subsubtopic: CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the privilege to rise in my place this morning, under Standing Order 106, and present a petition from quite a few people in my constituency who are totally opposed to the Government's proposed trade agreement with the United States.
They call upon the Government to dissolve the House and go to the people so that they can decide whether or not they want this trade deal.

subsubtopic: CANADA-U.S. FREE TRADE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my honour and duty to present a petition on behalf of a group of constituents from the Shellbrook-Canwood area near Prince Albert, Saskatchewan.
They suggest that since the Conservative Government has no mandate from the people of Canada to conclude the free trade agreement, the Government should go before the people of Canada in order to give them the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed free trade agreement during a national general election.

subsubtopic: HOMELESS-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the petitions that I am tabling today are signed by residents of Halifax; Rimouski; Winnipeg; Burlington; Crysler, Ontario; Summerside, Prince Edward Island; Florenceville, New Brunswick; Saint-Bruno; Laval; Greenfield Park; Pierrefonds and Laval-des-Rapides.
These petitioners deplore the fact that more than 100,000 people were homeless in Canada last year, that the number of homeless young people, women and whole families is steadily growing, that the number of affordable housing units is always decreasing and that the Government has not yet done anything to solve this problem.
For these reasons, the petitioners humbly ask Parliament to act immediately so that all Canadians can be given healthy, appropriate housing and that social programs be established so that these disadvantaged Canadians can re-enter Canadian society.

ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA Mr. Vic Althouse (Humboldt-Lake Centre) moved:
That this House urge the government to provide for emergency financial assistance to grain and livestock producers in the southern Prairies and in Central British Columbia in the event of a continuation of the current drought conditions in those areas, and to establish a long-term plan to deal with environmental disasters such as droughts, floods, and pest infestations.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion is put before the House today because of a disaster that seems to be looming but, more correctly, because those of us who have lived on the Prairies all our lives know that disasters do not occur necessarily this early in the season. It often appears very bleak in May and early June. Rains will turn that around. However, the statistics on this particular drought show that it is probably more all encompassing and more well entrenched than virtually any time previous in the history of recorded weather; and because the Government has said that as a result of the experience that we had with the 1985 drought it was to put into effect a longterm strategy to deal with such disasters. Since no long-term strategy was put into effect, we thought it would be desirable at this time to remind the House and the Government of the commitments that it made back then.
As you will recall, Mr. Speaker, in the speech to this House on November 27, 1985, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) who is still the Minister of Agriculture said, and 1 quote from Hansard, as reported at page 8869:
The $150 million program we are announcing today will provide immediate relief and we will continue our efforts to develop a long-term approach to emergency funding.
He went on to say, as reported at page 8870:
It is disruptive to producers to live with the uncertainty of not knowing what back-up assistance they will receive when natural disasters occur. Nor is it easy for the federal Government to take on substantial new financial commitments which have not been previously budgeted. That is why we are viewing the Crop Disaster Assistance Program as a field test for a permanent emergency assistance program which could be offered to farmers as a complement or extension to the current Crop Insurance Program.
Later in the year the Ministers of Agriculture for all provinces met. A national agriculture strategy was outlined. In that strategy it was pointed out that such a long-term disaster program was of great necessity.
Here we are in May of 1988 and no one knows what the long-term disaster program is because it has not been put into effect. That is the point of my motion today.
The data that are facing us are quite overwhelming. We have a drought of proportions not seen in western Canada for a long, long time. Some of the data that I have collected show that we are in a type of dry spell that has not been recorded very often in the 100 or more years of recorded history in terms of weather in that part of the country. We should notice that the threat of drought, given the current Environment Canada statistics, is that there is only about a 30 per cent chance of recovery this year. Thus we have less than one chance in three of getting lucky on this one.
To point out just how well ingrained this drought is, we should note statistics from the various recording stations in the country. In Saskatoon this is the worst drought that has been seen for 81 years. In Prince Albert it is the worst in 96 years. In Regina it is the worst in 88 years, and in Swift Current it is the worse in 101 years. This is not just a short-term drought of a few months' duration; it is a very well entrenched type of drought.
The people from Environment Canada point out what most of us know, that is, south of the Yellowhead Highway it is very dry. When one gets farther south of the No. 1 Highway, which covers about 35 per cent to 40 per cent of the prairie grain belt, it is described as really, really dry. When one looks at the record of the small communities and the farmers who are trying to cope with this lack of moisture that has been building for close to a year now, one sees that the dug-outs are going empty.
For a big chunk of the territory about which I am speaking, in particular Palliser's Triangle, it is very difficult to strike water for wells. Surface moisture must be relied upon, and there is no surface moisture. There was no surface moisture in the soil last fall. All small sloughs and potholes have gone dry, as have many small lakes. Farmers were pumping water from whatever sources they could find to their dug-outs close to home, as were towns and villages. Many of those are now down to 10 per cent or 20 per cent available water supplies from reservoirs.
Governments cannot make water. They cannot create it. However, they can by setting out long-range programs to work out methods of coping with a shortage of water. The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration has been doing that to
May 9, 1988

some extent ever since a very bad drought in the 1930s. It has been supplying long pipelines and large pumps to transfer water from where it exists to where it is needed. The options are very limited. There are not very many sources left.
The problem is not limited only to the Palliser's Triangle in the Prairies or the area south of the Yellowhead Highway. It has extended with a vengeance into central British Columbia. To give Hon. Members some idea of this, I wish to quote from a couple of reports. An official from the Quilchena area, a spokesman for the Vernon irrigation district, said that they can only operate at about half supply this year. Five mountain reservoirs feeding the Vernon district stand at 10 per cent of capacity and are not expected to climb about 50 per cent during the melt and run-off. The official said: "We cannot create water, no matter what the public thinks we can do as a Government".
In the forest area foresters point out that the lack of moisture can create a very bad fire season this year. This will occur because some of the logs that are lying on the bed of the forest are now drying out and are becoming very combustible. This makes it easy for a forest fire to get started and to carry. This will have an effect on the tourist industry.
British Columbians in the central part of the province are already predicting a reduction in tourism, as they are expecting they will need bans on campfires and camping in the forest areas which attract people to that part of the country. As well, fishing lakes are now losing the volume of water they have and many lakes are significantly lower this year. The lower water levels result in more fish dying off. As well, it makes it very difficult for them to spawn and to move upstream. It is impossible for a fish to move up a stream that does not exist any more. Thus the long-term effects on the environment in that part of the country are quite scary as well.
On the Prairies the lack of surface water will have a longterm effect on the amount of wildlife that survives, particularly water-fowl that use the prairie region as their major flight path. Many species also use it as their major nesting site, including Canada geese and field duck. A great many of those species have their traditional nesting sites in farming areas on the Prairies.
We are concerned that the Government has failed to provide a long-term financial plan to deal with disasters such as those that occur with drought, flood, massive forest fires, or an influx of grasshoppers or other forms pestilence. The Government could have done something about that, but it has failed to do anything even though it promised to be back in the fall of 1985.
Apparently the Government has also not paid very much attention to the long-term trends that the Department of the Environment points out is a reality. I am speaking now of the greenhouse effect. Most Members in the House will know that is an effect that scientists have discovered over the past 10 or
Supply
15 years. It has resulted in a layer of carbon dioxide being formed in the stratosphere. As forests and fossilized fuels burn they create carbon dioxide which has not been recycled in the normal manner by the breathing of plants and trees to utilize the carbon dioxide and transpire oxygen. As forests disappear and the burning of carbon fuels increases, a surplus of carbon dioxide has been produced which has created a layer that has tended to trap the heat from the sun within the earth's atmosphere. That has been slowly raising the mean temperatures of the earth.
Environmental experts tell us that in Canada this will mean an increase of mean temperature from 2° to 5° centigrade depending on which part of the country one is speaking of. Of most pertinence to this dissertation is that the prairie region, particularly Palliser's Triangle and central British Columbia, will be the areas that appear to be most likely to reap the benefit, if one can call it that, of the 5° temperature.
According to scientific projections, this will come into full being somewhere around the year 2000 or 2010. I believe at the present time we are seeing the beginning of that phenomenon in Palliser's Triangle of the Pairies and in central British Columbia. This particular drought will not go away easily, but we will be faced with these high temperatures and limited rainfalls that are projected as the greenhouse effect exacerbates in those regions of the country.
This effect will require a massive change in technique for people to survive in that region. It will require some assistance from federal and provincial Governments. I think that the Ministers of Agriculture for the provinces and for the federal Government were correct in 1985 when their assessment was that there should be a long-term agricultural strategy which would take this effect into account. I regret that that strategy has not been put in place, and no long-term funding has been established on the part of the federal Government or in conjunction with the provinces in order to address these types of long-term issues. The answers will not be found by simply sitting back in a rainier part of the country and observing those areas with telescopes, preparing reports, or attending in the areas. Stringent scientific work will have to be done to delineate the problem. There will have to be recourse to the engineering and ecological knowledge that we presently have to make better use of moisture supplies in those areas in order that they do not turn into the semi-desert that the greenhouse effect is projected to have on those particular regions.
As I mentioned when I commenced by speech, 35 to 45 per cent of prairie grain land lies in this region; much of the fruit belt in the Okanagan is dependent on the water supplies that are generated in central British Columbia, as are the beef industry and the grazing industry, very large parts of the agricultural component of central British Columbia. As the pastures dry up and the water disappears, there will be less chance of producing calves and beef in that area. A reduction of 50 per cent in the water reservoirs will make it very difficult to keep the apple and soft fruit industries alive and healthy in that part of the region.

This particular drought is not only isolated to Palliser's Triangle in the Prairies; it goes much beyond that. I submit that because this is a well entrenched system and it has been well defined by international scientists that the greenhouse effect will be with us for a long time until the earth can be reforested and the consumption of fossilized fuels is reduced. Therefore, a long-term solution and plan developed if we are to keep populations on that semi-arid part of the Prairies as it turns into a semi-desert.
The Government was remiss in not acting upon its own good advice in 1985. I close my remarks by reminding the Government that it has neglected to handle the wealth of the country in a proper manner by putting water wells and collection sites in place in the intervening years. It has been remiss in not taking seriously the drought situation on the central Prairies and in central British Columbia. This motion draws the matter to the attention of the country and of the Government in order that the Government can correct its lack of policy for the last two and a half years.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution before us today concerning the prairie drought situation calls upon the Government to take two actions. The first part of the motion seeks to provide emergency assistance to the Prairies facing the worst drought in a hundred years. The second part of the motion calls upon the Government to put in place longterm programs to deal with the drought situation.
As the Hon. Member from Saskatchewan has already indicated, the Government should have known in 1984 and 1985 that we were not dealing with a casual occurrence of an occasional drought. Clearly there have been two important influences on world weather patterns. The El Ningo effect which caused tremendous drought in the Sahel region of Africa has had its influence in the last year or so in the prairie regions. That is a cyclical event; it comes along from time to time. But more important is the long-term problem of the greenhouse effect of warming of temperatures due to increased carbon dioxide in the upper atmosphere.
I am very conscious of the issue because in the fall of 1986 in my own constituency, which is on the shore of Lake Huron and has the same water table levels as Lake Erie and Lake Michigan, there was the highest water levels in 100 years. Yet one year later, in the fall of 1987, there was a drop of some two and a half feet in the lake level of Lake Huron, Lake Michigan, Lake Erie, and the compensating effect on Lake Superior,
Only through a tremendous increase in temperatures generally, with a corresponding reduction in moisture levels, could we have experienced a drop in the level of the Great Lakes Basin of some two and a half feet to three feet. The western Prairies have been hit by the same kind of reduction in moisture levels and the same kind of increased evaporation rate due to warmer temperatures, resulting in the lowest
moisture levels in 100 years. The last time the western Prairies and certain areas of B.C. experienced moisture levels comparable with those being experienced today was in 1889.
The motion now being debated calls upon the Government to take appropriate action to deal with this emergency, and to put in place longer term mechanisms to deal with the drier prairie conditions being experienced.
I had occasion this morning to speak with a farmer in southern Alberta, who told me that the actual top soil was dry to a level of two and one-half to three feet. Given the total lack of ground moisture, the small showers that they do experience have practically no impact.
I had occasion last week to talk with some long time residents of southern Alberta, individuals who speak from actual experience when they speak of the drought of the 1930s, and they feel uncertain about the current situation. While everyone hopes that the present lack of moisture is a temporary situation, time is running out for this year's crop. Livestock operations are equally affected. Clearly, if there is no substantial rainfall by mid-May, summer pastures will be irretrievably damaged. Without sufficient moisture, we even face the possibility of grains not germinating.
I should like to quote from an article on the prairie drought which appeared in The Ottawa Citizen of May 2, 1988, as follows:
Since last summer, parts of Western Canada, especially in southern Saskatchewan and Alberta, have had only about 50 per cent of normal precipitation. Some areas have received only one quarter.
That confirms the kinds of effects we have seen in other parts of the country.
The article goes on to quote a Mr. Allan Moore of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration, as follows:
"I think it's as dry, if not drier, than the Dirty '30s," said Allan Moore of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration in the nearby town of Gravelbourg, Sask.
"It's so dry, the land is just like a sponge".
There was also an article in The Globe and Mail of May 2, 1988. The article is datelined as originating from Tilley, Alberta, with the headline being: "Albertans bracing for drought".
The article quotes Mr. Thomas Jensen, of Alberta Agriculture as follows:
"They're all sitting out there waiting, debating whether to seed. If we don't get rain in May it could be a catastrophe. But it's not just Alberta. There is a similar situation in California, Montana, Utah and Idaho. It's a continental thing.''
And, of course, the "they're" refers to the agricultural producers.
A recent press release dealt with the desertification of the world, areas which are becoming drier, and drier, and drier. The maps which accompanied that press release showed
May 9, 1988

eastern B.C. and the southern parts of Alberta and Saskatchewan as being among those areas which are becoming more and more desert-like.
The farm producers to whom I have spoken say that dug-outs are dry; that there is no spring run-off, and no possibility of those dug-outs, which are so important in terms of cattle operations, being filled this year. For the first time, many wells have run dry. In many areas of southern Alberta, one can go down to two and one-half to three feet without finding any moisture whatsoever.
We are experiencing one of the driest periods in the history of western Canada and, while we all hope that it will be of a temporary nature, clearly the Government must now indicate the type of emergency system that will be provided, whether it be by way of dug-out construction, the drilling of wells, the construction of water pipelines, or other measures.
The Government of Alberta has already indicated that it is prepared to provide some $20 million for the purpose of making emergency supplies of water available to these areas.
The second matter to be addressed is the provision of feed supplies for livestock. The situation in respect of grain crops will become clearer toward the end of this month, and certainly by early June. We may be faced with a situation of there being insufficient moisture to bring about germination.
The producers to whom I have spoken in the last week stress the need for a livestock assistance program on an urgent basis. They need to have a commitment from the Government on what it is prepared to do.
To sum up, what the western agricultural community needs is a commitment that there be provision for making emergency water supplies available, together with a commitment to address the ongoing problem of water shortages, and a commitment in respect of emergency supplies of feed to support the livestock.
In some areas of Manitoba, cattle can be moved to feedlots. However, that is not a solution for southern Alberta and Saskatchewan. It is simply not possible. The grass supply in the community pastures in southern Alberta and southern Saskatchewan is such that those pastures are refusing to accept any cattle. That is a first for those areas of the country.
In addition to the drought, the western agricultural community continues to face the whole farm debt problem, the insolvency of the Farm Credit Corporation itself, and the dropping of land values.
These are all matters that need to be addressed. In addition, the higher Canadian dollar vis-a-vis the U.S. dollar leads to lower prices, the reason being, of course, that most farm commodities are traded in U.S. dollars.
Clearly, there are a number of ongoing problems facing the agricultural community. Maintaining interest rates in Canada at 2.5 per cent above the American rate pushes the Canadian dollar up in value vis-a-vis the U.S. dollar. I suppose that is
Supply
part of the "gentleman's handshake" on the Canada-U.S. trade deal. The result, of course, is that we end up with lower effective prices for Canadian livestock, together with higher interest rates.
What has the Government's response been to date, Mr. Speaker? In answer to a question which I put to the Minister, he said that he would probably be answering the need for additional assistance for water supplies and would consider taking money from the long-term soil conservation fund which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced last December. He did not give any indication whether the full amount of the funding would be made available. The $75 million is a cost-shared program. Alberta has already made a commitment of $20 million. If the federal Government were to do the same, I suppose there would be enough in that fund, but it has not yet been indicated what the Government has not yet indicated what it will do. It seems to me this is an emergency and that we should not be taking funds out of the long time soil conservation and degradation fund. It seems to me that we have a contingency fund of a couple of billion dollars. That is from where the funds should be coming so we can get on with the long-term soil conservation and degradation program as has been done in other years when we faced this same kind of problem.
So far there is no clear commitment of assistance to move feed into the drought areas. There is no clear commitment as far as I can see on the number of dollars for emergency water supply funding or for emergency systems such as expanding or developing new dug-outs, wells, or pipeline systems. Equally important in the long run is the need for long-term expansion of PFRA funding for the water management program, to put in place measures and programs for improved water storage, new wells, and so on. We should have increased funding for that because this does not appear to be a short-term policy.
In the Minister's press statement of November, 1985, he indicated that the Government was working toward a longterm disaster assistance program in place of this year's plan. In the agriculture committee meeting a couple of nights ago, when the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer) was asked whether the Government was going to put in place a long-term program, he said that it was difficult to have an ongoing emergency planning operation. By definition, if it is an emergency, it is pretty tough to know what it is one should be doing. Whether the Government will put in place a long-term emergency program is clearly not apparent at this time.
We need today a commitment from the Minister that, if the emergency continues to develop, there will be systems on an equalized basis for pipelines, for emergency dug-out development, for water supplies, and so on, as well as a commitment of funding for the provision of feed in the drought areas. That would strengthen prices which have dropped for stock cows and cow and calf operators at this time.

May 9, 1988
Supply
Those issues must be faced because long-term problems require time to develop fully. Clearly there is a need in the southern Prairies for more long-term water storage management and funding for the PFRA. From the presentation made last week by the various farm groups, such as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, funds under the PFRA program are totally committed for this year. We need long-term funding for a consistent policy of developing water storage for irrigation. We may have to face this in the future. We may have to change the types of crops that are grown in some areas of the southern Prairies. We know that with the PFRA program projects have been put in place which ensure water supply and have made a big difference this year. Some farmers have been able to irrigate crop land and can seed a crop. That is perhaps not a first, but it is rare. Usually the irrigation system is used to supply moisture at a later stage, not just for the seeding operation itself.
These are urgent issues and I hope the Minister will be able to give a clear commitment of the Government's plan in this regard. The western drought situation, on top of the whole downturn in the oil industry and the whole downturn in commodity prices for grain, is leading to a big disaster. The West is waiting to know exactly how much of a commitment the Government is prepared to make to meet this emergency, to maintain livestock herds, and ultimately to provide assistance for the grain crops if and when that becomes necessary.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there any questions or comments? Debate. The Flon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise).

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this occasion for the House to pay attention to and examine the serious water conditions in western Canada and in certain parts of the Province of British Columbia.
I want to assure Members opposite, indeed all Members of the House, as well as all primary producers, and others in the agri-food industry that our Government is fully aware of the situation. The Prairies are faced with low soil moisture reserves, low spring run-offs, and virtually no rain to speak of.
Most areas of southern Alberta, southern Saskatchewan, and the southwest portion of Manitoba are those areas most seriously affected. Topsoil is dry in many locations. Dug-outs and water supplies for livestock are low. The below average quantity of snowpack in the mountains is a cause of concern for irrigation districts and for producers who rely heavily-and some rely exclusively-on irrigation for crop success.
In the Province of British Columbia, a serious lack of water this year may-and I underline the word may-affect livestock producers in the central and southern ranching areas and fruit producers in the Okanagan Valley. In some cases, below normal water levels have been experienced for several consecutive years. We are fully aware of these conditions, as are, I hope, most Members of the House. It is obvious, of course, that some Members are not aware of the considerable effort the federal Government is expending right now, even as
I speak here today, to deal with these adverse conditions in western Canada.
We are actively monitoring the situation in co-operation with the provinces, and there are federal-provincial drought committees in each of the affected provinces. A special Agriculture Canada task force has been working for several weeks now to assess conditions and to look at the adequacy of our present programs. In fact, just last night, there was a meeting of Deputy Ministers, my Deputy Minister and his counterparts in the western provinces. I am pleased to say that the Assistant Deputy Ministers' committee is being formed to work with Agriculture Canada's task force and the provincial drought committees. They will advise Ministers, both federal and provincial, on a daily basis.
We are acting and we are responding. We have safety net programs in place to deal with the situation. We already have a framework for action to deal with drought and similar disasters. There are a number of elements in that framework.
The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration, of course, is one of these elements, and a very important one. Since 1935, PFRA has been at work developing rural water supplies and conserving prairie topsoil. The federal Government set up PFRA to respond to the terrible conditions in the Dirty Thirties. Its job was to ensure that communities and producers got water when they needed it and to ensure that soil would not blow away and turn them into another dust bowl.
The PFRA continues to this day to develop water supplies to help drought-proof the Prairies, no small task. It has been a lot of work, but it has been a bona fide success story. Because the PFRA people are working very closely with the provinces to monitor the soil and weather conditions, we are ensuring that we get the maximum mileage out of our complementary water programs. We are providing technical assistance and advice. Pumping equipment is also being utilized. Of course, there are community pastures which are proving to be especially useful, and helpful, at this time.
PFRA will spend about $7.2 million on its rural water development program this year. It will help farmers dig wells, plan dug-outs, as it will help with stock-watering dams, and irrigation projects. In fact, since 1935, more than 165,000 farmers have obtained assistance for these projects from this program.
Grants and advice are available to groups of farmers wanting to build common reservoirs for irrigation projects. Small communities can receive financial and technical help for developing water sources and water resources.
Over the years, PFRA has built more than 100 major dams, reservoirs, and irrigation works. There is the Gardner Dam-Lake Diefenbaker project, built at a cost of some $100 million. More recently, there has been the Weyburn Dam in Saskatchewan, the Carseland Dam, the Brooks Aqueduct and the
May 9, 1988

rehabilitated Bassano Dam in Alberta, and finally, the raising of the PFRA dam in Morden, Manitoba. These activities demonstrate the federal commitment to providing water to the ever thirsty Prairies.
In British Columbia, action is under way to use the federal-provincial agri-food development agreement, or ARDSA as it is called, to develop better long-term water supplies. We are working with the local irrigation districts in fruit growing areas to divert new supplies to reservoirs or to lower dam projects.
Very importantly, we are working to conserve water by using available supplies as effectively and efficiently as possible. In the cattle regions of British Columbia, we are looking at perhaps extending the ARDSA to help cover on-farm water supply projects such as digging wells. Cattle producers, fruit growers, and other farmers have the continued support of the federal Government as they seek solutions to their water problems.
It is clear that we are taking steps to deal with the present situation which is a water shortage situation, not a crop drought situation, as this debate will indicate today. We are working co-operatively with the provinces and with the producers. We will do what we can to ensure that our present programs help out as much as possible.
I am pleased that the motion before the House recognizes that additional measures are not necessary at this time. It is too early to speak of losing crops or of losing livestock. Agriculture Canada's research scientists are advising farmers on how to deal with the current soil and water situation.
For instance, the Lethbridge research station advises that the season is still early. Adequate and timely rainfall between now and August will still ensure a good harvest. I understand that the problem area has already been reduced in Manitoba as a result of rain on the weekend. There was also rain in certain parts of southeastern Saskatchewan, the Estevan and the Weyburn areas. It is too early to make predictions.
The motion before us asks the Government to establish a long-term plan to deal with emergencies like drought. I wonder if opposition Members have an appreciation of what PFRA has been doing in that specific area for the last 53 years: in two words, drought-proofing; in a phrase, making the prairie farming community more stable and viable. However, what happens in those years when crops are still hit by drought or some other disaster like floods or pests? We have a long-term plan to deal with crop failures. Again, in two words, it is crop insurance.
In 1959, the Crop Insurance Act was passed by the federal Government, and since then we have been providing to farmers a way of protecting them against crop losses. It is a vital element in our over-all strategy because there are now some 230 different insurance plans for the 87 crops that are covered across Canada. In 1987, some 134,000 farmers participated and more than 42 million acres were covered.
Supply
The federal Government contributes 50 per cent of the premiums in all provinces with the exception of Newfoundland and Quebec. In these provinces it pays 25 per cent and half of the administrative costs. In no province does a farmer pay more than 50 per cent of the premium.
In fact, last year, the federal Government paid some $181.5 million toward farmers' premiums and it was money well spent. It provides the kind of protection needed in the risky business of farming, and this Government is committed to crop insurance as the main way to hedge our bets against the whims of Mother Nature.
Let us look at the drought years of 1984 and 1985. For those two years a total of some $24 million was paid out in the Province of British Columbia, $79 million in the Province of Manitoba, $487 million in the Province of Alberta, and some $640 million in the Province of Saskatchewan. That is an awful lot of protection, but it was not perfect, so in 1984 and 1985 the federal Government paid a total of $75 million in livestock drought assistance. In November of 1985 we announced a $ 150-million prairie crop drought assistance program.
After these special measures, we took a hard look at crop insurance to see whether or not it was doing the job adequately. Indeed, the federal Government and the provinces agreed that it was doing a good job of covering crop losses at a reasonable cost. However, the federal and provincial Agriculture Ministers agreed that additional protection should be provided to meet widespread successive losses. This was so that special measures would not be required again.
More crops across Canada are now insurable, and in western Canada major improvements have been made. There is expanded and improved feed security-forage insurance and there is now a multi-year disaster benefit. We made special efforts this year to publicize the deadlines for both forage and crop insurance. I can report that western farmers, particularly livestock and forage producers, have responded quite positively. Not only is the number of farmers insured for forage up by 60 per cent, farmers have purchased some 130 per cent more protection. Increased participation is also expected for crop insurance. In short, we have long-term measures in place to deal with disasters. We have PFRA. We have all-risk crop insurance. Just as important, particularly at this very trying time for Canadian farmers, especially those in western Canada, we have the record of commitment by this Government.
Since September, 1984 federal spending on agriculture increased by over 400 per cent. In 1986, we introduced the Special Canadian Grains Program, the largest federal farm initiative in the history of the country. We put $1 billion into the pockets of grains and oilseeds farmers reeling from the effects of the international subsidy war. Again, in 1987 we outdid ourselves by extending the program another year,

May 9, 1988
Supply
seeking an additional $1.1 billion for farmers. About $975 million of that is for western producers.
Last month, my colleague, the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds, announced a western grain stabilization interim payment of some $695 million, but that is not all. We are also writing down $750 million of the Western Grain Stabilization Fund deficit. We have extended the farm fuel tax rebate program until 1991. We put more money into the Farm Debt Review Boards, and we are providing additional funding to the Farm Credit Corporation.
On the specific subject of soil and water conservation, we announced a $75 million national soil and conservation program to prevent losses of our most precious resource. In the dry conditions being experienced in parts of the West right now, the need for soil conservation becomes all that much more important. We cannot let our future blow away.
Those are just some of the things which show the Government's commitment to Canadian farmers. I think that upon assessment by any fair-minded individual the record speaks for itself. The farmers of Canada know this Government has gone to bat for them and will continue to do so, both on the domestic and the international scene. They know we have supported them with technical and financial assistance. They know we have supported them with long-term development programs like PFRA and safety nets like the Western Grain Stabilization Fund. With the renovation and updating of crop insurance, they know they have the ongoing protection from disaster they need to continue in the business of farming.
In conclusion, we have built a sound foundation for the future. Our aim is a prosperous, stable agriculture industry in western Canada, indeed in all provinces and regions of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the Minister could indicate whether there will be a specific amount of money allocated for emergency water supplies. As I understand the situation, the most urgent need is for a commitment regarding emergency water supplies and funds for livestock feed. In 1984, I believe it was, the Government provided a direct payment of about $30 per stock cow. The Minister mentioned in the House on May 4 that he was prepared to take funds out of the long-term soil conservation and degradation program for emergency water supplies. Is the Minister indicating that he is prepared to match the amounts allocated, for example, by Alberta of $20 million for wells and dug-outs and pipelines? Is he prepared to indicate what the funding will be?
In addition, the Minister mentioned the all risk crop insurance. Does that preclude special assistance, as well, for grain producers who may not be fully covered by that insurance? I realize, of course, that question will not be fully canvassed until we receive information about the crop situation much later this year.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want the Hon. Member to take exception to my response. He has put some pretty good questions to me, but I am not so sure that they are not hypothetical. However, that is somewhat immaterial. What is important is that they are premature.
He talked about the emergency, the response I gave to him the other day with respect to the $75 million soil and water conservation program, and whether the revised crop insurance program would preclude any additional measures. I can only say at this point that the federal-provincial task force is continuing its job. It will do so on a day-to-day basis. As in the past, as things develop, at the proper time, and when they are in a position to assess the seriousness of the situation and report with certain recommendations to which we can respond in a reasonable and effective manner, then and only then will I be in a position to respond to those questions. I think the Hon. Member knows exactly what I have in mind.
When I responded to him in the House, I believe it was last week, with reference to the $75 million I meant this and nothing more. When we have an emergency situation, sometimes common sense and good judgment dictates that we change our priorities. First, I hope Mother Nature looks upon us favourably. Second, I hope it will not be necessary to respond with any special program because I hope ongoing programs meet the need. Consequently, I hope it will not be necessary for us, even during an emergency, to readjust our priorities so that perhaps we might have to consider taking money from that fund.
It is an important subject. We lose $1 billion worth of topsoil a year. We could not sit by as a Government and do nothing. We have been doing a fair amount through PFRA, of course, but because of its importance it needed additional funds.
Discussions have been ongoing between PFRA and the various provinces. In most areas, particularly western Canada, we are reaching the position where we are just about ready to sign accords with the various provinces. They can match dollar for dollar, and consequently we will have $150 million in funding in that area.
In response to his last question with regard to whether or not it will preclude it, that will depend on a number of factors. Even though participation in crop insurance has been at an alltime high, we will have to await the assessment of that federal-provincial task force. When it sends its recommendations to us we will respond.

Mr. Speaker, in the Minister's response to the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) he mentioned that he believed he is about to be able to sign accords with the various provinces regarding to a long-term strategy. What has caused the delay over the past two and a half years? Did it take another imminent drought to get all the parties back to the bargaining table? What has been the delay since the national
May 9, 1988

agricultural strategy was agreed to by the 10 First Ministers of Agriculture and the federal Minister himself?
The intention of all parties concerned seemed to be very clear. What has taken so long to get the four western agriculture Ministers to read an agreement? Was it not prepared until the drought became more imminent and the disaster became more real, or were there technical considerations in the way? What is responsible for the two and a half year time lag?

Mr. Speaker, there was not a two and a half year time lag. The Hon. Member refers to the national agricultural strategy. That, of course, was one document. Our $75 million soil and water conservation program was announced and made available when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) spoke in December at the Agricultural Outlook Conference. December 1987, is not two and a half years ago. There has been no delay in this program at all.
Subsequent to that announcement in December PFRA officials began their negotiations with various counterparts across the country. Therefore, the contrary would indeed be the case. Significant progress has been made and was only made when we put that $75 million in the window, with the condition that it had to be matched by provincial funds. That made a lot of sense because agriculture is a shared and joint responsibility. In land use and matters more closely related to soil and water conservation one will find that there is an awful lot of provincial jurisdictional responsibility. If you do not think so, just challenge the provinces on that particular aspect.
The only way to make progress in that area is to put up some dollars, identify the problem as a serious one, and tell the provinces that as they have a responsibility as well they should match our dollars; then, at the end of the day, we will have $150 million which we can invest in this specific area.

I take it from the Minister's answer that he was referring in his remarks only to the soil and water program rather than to the long-term crop disaster fund about which I thought he was talking; he sort of mixed the two together in his response.
I would like to shift to the central British Columbia problem with its low snow melt and shrinking reservoirs, some of which are at less than 50 per cent levels. Since those reservoirs are also being used as part of the water supply which provides power through an international river into the United States, could the Minister list for us what the priorities will be from the Canadian side with regard to power requirements, human use, food growers' use, cattlemen's use, watering lawns, and so on? Is there a priority list for usage? I would think that there must be some such plan in existence, since the problem existed last year as well and appears to be getting even worse this year.

Mr. Speaker, that is a timely and excellent question. I wish that I were in a position today to respond accurately and in detail to the Hon. Member. I am somewhat cautious to do so in the time available. While there may well be no question in my mind about what the priorities should
Supply
be-and I think common sense would dictate that-I am cautious about listing them at this time because we may well be precluded by some international agreement. I would at least want to have the opportunity to check whether such an international agreement exists. I am quite certain that it does. I am sure that it is public information. I will be seeking that information and, when I find it, I will be happy to share it with the Hon. Member.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words in this debate about drought on the Prairies. I want to address my comments for a few minutes to a different area, that is, farm stress.
I came back from my constituency about a week ago where I attended 12 public meetings in the last four or five days of April. Some were in farmers' houses to which they invited their neighbours and friends to get about 15 or 20 farmers together. I was able to acquire a very good understanding of the situation farmers are facing.
As the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) knows, the drought problem is not as acute in my riding as it is in some, as my riding is a bit more toward the northeast. In fact, in the northern part of my riding, which is near Swan River, Manitoba, they have a bit too much rain. Mr. Speaker, you may have seen on the news that Swan River has a bit of flooding, and that comes into my riding a bit. However, when one gets further south near the City of Yorkton one starts running into the drought problems, and the farther southwest one goes toward Regina the more severe it becomes. Therefore, while the drought is a problem in my riding, it is not as severe as it is in the south near Swift Current and Moose Jaw.
However, we must do whatever we can to relieve what I call the farm crisis in general. In addition to the drought there is an economic crisis facing farmers. There are the grain wars between the Europeans and the United States. There has been a tremendous drop in farm income. A large part of farm income is now received from farm stabilization plans, the Western Grain Stabilization Plan, deficiency payments, and other such things. As a result of economic hardship and the very severe drought, there is now a great deal of stress and emotional problems for farmers right across the prairie basin.
My colleagues from Humboldt-Lake Centre and Algoma mentioned many of the statistical realities of the drought- farm income going down, water reservoirs going down, dug-outs drying up, shallow wells drying up, the need to dig deeper wells, what is going to happen to the crops, the greenhouse effect, and the semi-arid part of the southern prairie belt which will turn into a quasi-desert if this situation continues.
We all know what happened in the 1930s as a result of the drought. Behind those headlines and those realities is another reality, that is, the tremendous stress upon the farmer and the families involved in this kind of an economic crisis. I want to spend a few minutes speaking about that this morning. I hope

May 9, 1988
Supply
we can start thinking about what we can do to help farmers out of this situation.
Behind the headlines there is a great feeling of despair, a great feeling of helplessness, and a great feeling of hopelessness for the many thousands of farm families in the southern part of the prairie belt. A very recent study was commissioned by the provincial Government of Saskatchewan into the whole area of farm stress. The study by the Burgam Consulting Company talked about the tremendous increase in alcoholism, depression, family violence, suicide, drugs, and so on, with respect to farmers. I want to suggest that we all take a look at some of the findings. I have here a copy of the May 2 edition of the Regina Leader-Post which gives a very good report of the study conducted on this question. It talks about alcoholism being on the increase and how depression is increasing because of what is happening on the Prairies, not just because of drought but because of economic hardship in general. I would like to quote Derrell Rodine of Weyburn who, for a number of years, has conducted farm stress workshops across Saskatchewan. He says that many of the problems are as a result of shattered dreams. He states:
"You get married and have lots of dreams," Rodine said.
"When things begin to fall apart there are feelings of guilt and a person tends to turn on the people they love."
Every day Rodine sees the toll that tough economic times are taking on farm families.
"Some farmers are carrying an immense burden of guilt for not being able to manage their land well in either physical or financial terms," he said.
Many fall into a form of "psychological paralysis" and are unable to work.
While many rural people are under a great deal of stress and some have been pushed into depression, a few fall into the ultimate depression and take their own lives.
Two years ago 26 people killed themselves.
"I had a woman come up to me in tears-she said her husband stopped the combine in the middle of the field, got off and shot himself," he said.
The aftershocks of suicide rip through a family and the community, leaving scars that often never heal.
These are signals of what is happening right now across rural Canada. I am not sure whether the federal Government can provide more leadership on the problem of farm stress, but perhaps when I complete my remarks in a few moments, the Minister of Agriculture can make a response in the period for questions and comments whether or not there is any new initiative the Government is contemplating in terms of farm stress.
I want to refer to another study that was done by the University of Manitoba, which indicated that farmers in financial crisis suffer more stress than a police officer three days after a shooting incident. When I first saw that headline I found it hard to believe, but I would like to read the very short article that summarizes this particular state:
Financially troubled farmers face higher levels of stress than police officers in shooting incidents, according to a Brandon University study.
And farming is ranked in the top 10 per cent of high stress occupations, according to studies carried out in the United States.
The Manitoba farmers, interviewed for the Brandon study, suffer from headaches, marriage problems and irritability at a greater rate than Royal Canadian Mounted Police officers contacted within three days of a shooting incident, said the study by James and Lily Walker of the university.
Another study by the Walkers said 11 per cent of Prairie farmers had considered suicide. Meanwhile, a survey in north-central Saskatchewan found that 80 per cent of farm families exhibited signs of stress.
For their First study, the Walkers interviewed 643 Manitoba farmers and compared the results with a study of 56 RCMP officers involved in shooting incidents.
They found that 16 per cent of the farmers had increased their consumption of alcohol, compared with nine per cent of the RCMP officers.
Twenty-seven per cent of the farmers reported marriage problems compared with two per cent of the police officers and 58 per cent of the farmers experienced sleeplessness compared with 50 per cent of the police officers.
In addition, 78 per cent of the farmers said they were irritable and losing their temper, compared with 11 per cent of the police officers.
This is the result of a study conducted by Brandon University about the relative problems of stress between police officers after a shooting incident, which is a pretty serious thing, and farmers in severe financial difficulty. The stress level is higher for farmers living under severe financial difficulties. I think these kinds of studies point out in very vivid detail that there is a real crisis in rural Canada, particularly in prairie Canada where it is compounded by the drought situation which is forcing many, many farmers to the wall in terms of their very survival. There are increasing rates of suicide, drug abuse, alcoholism, depression, emotional problems, and so on. It is also creating very serious community problems.
When there is a crisis like this more and more farmers leave the land. We can see this in my riding and in many other rural ridings in western Canada. More and more people leave the small towns, and then the whole fabric of community organizations start to deteriorate and disappear. The people who are left feel more and more isolated because many of their friends have moved away to large towns and cities. Many of the services in these rural communities start to disappear because the population base drops, and of course the economic infusion drops. There are fewer people to support community events and activities. There are fewer people to organize sporting events, social events, and so on. In many ways the community itself then starts to re-enforce the depression and stress the farmer is facing, and people become very isolated. That is the very, very serious social problem facing many farmers in Prairie Canada today.
I referred to a series of excellent articles in the May 2 edition of the Leader-Post. It might be worth while reading it. It is a summary of the stress study done by the provincial Government of Saskatchewan and the University of Manitoba. There is also a reference to what is being done in the United States in terms of farm problems.
Also in the same newspaper is an article under the headline "Alcoholism Exacting a High Price in Rural Saskatchewan". It concerns the tremendous increase in alcoholism related to
May 9, 1988

the economic and drought crisis now plaguing farmers in rural Saskatchewan. In some ways the very occupation of farming, because one is alone so much of the time, makes alcoholism a lot easier than in other occupations where one is working more closely with others. The farmer is often alone. He goes out on the combine or tractor, or he goes out to check the cattle. It is very easy to consume a mickey of hard alcohol, or even 26 ounces of hard alcohol, and be able to hide it from his family and friends. He can hide his problem a lot easier than if he was a teacher at elementary or high school. Alcoholism is a way of forgetting some of the economic problems one has.
I do not want to go on at great length and repeat the facts placed on the record today by my friends, the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), and the Minister himself. We all know there is a very serious problem in terms of drought in western Canada. We all know there is a very serious economic problem in terms of the grain wars around the world. We all know there is financial insecurity, deterioration of rural communities, and so on.
What I want to do this morning is point out some of the human consequences and tragedies behind the headlines of the newspapers and behind the television footage we see in terms of the crisis facing farmers. I was wondering if the Minister would get up in the question and comment period to tell us what his thoughts are about farm stress. Perhaps he could elaborate on what we could be doing as a Parliament and what he could be doing as the Minister to provide some type of support, more than what we already have provided to help farmers who are in this type of situation.
I know that he has been doing something in terms of initiative and in terms of the drought question itself. There are committees now at work. He has talked about various financial solutions. All these items are, of course, very helpful. I am wondering whether or not the Minister can add more in order to offer some hope to those facing farm stress crisis.
I want to underline that this is a very serious problem. We all hope, of course, as the Minister said, that Mother Nature intervenes to solve the problem for us. But that will not necessarily happen. Even if it does happen, the world trade wars which create financial crises, have created a lot of stress for the farmers of this country.
I will stop there and invite in a rather bizarre way the Minister to comment on these matters, or perhaps to ask me a question as a way of telling us what he is thinking about in terms of farm stress.

Mr. Speaker, I said when I began my speech a few minutes ago that I welcomed the occasion in the House to assess the potential drought problems in western Canada. Of course, I certainly do welcome the debate today. The lead-off spokesman for the Official Opposition and also the spokesman
Supply
for the New Democratic Party were somewhat premature in dealing with the subject-matter today.
However, I want to compliment the previous speaker, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), for taking his time to touch on a very serious problem which exists today. More than likely, unfortunately, it will persist in the country for some time in the future. I suppose I am here to make certain that I respond. If there were no response it might leave the impression, the very false impression, that we were not aware of the situation related to stress that exists in certain sectors of the farm community. I hope the Hon. Member will appreciate that one can hardly be the Minister of Agriculture of Canada and not be aware of the tragic events in the primary sector, particularly during a time when certain sectors of the industry, primarily grains and oilseeds, are facing the toughest times ever in 50 years.
One observation I want to make is with respect to the fact that we often talk only about the stress on farmers. It is true that farmers have stress, but I wonder if we ever stop and think about on whose shoulders and in whose heart and mind that stress really ends up. It is at least shared. I think the heaviest share probably falls in the heart and mind and in the lap of the farm wife. This is why we have given a much higher priority to the concerns and day-to-day problems that have been overlooked and ignored for decades by previous Governments and how those problems and concerns relate to farm women.
Farm women have been the unsung heroes of the primary sector of the agricultural industry in Canada and, indeed, in many other countries I suppose going back to day one. We have been dissatisfied with that. We have given them a much higher profile. Indeed, we have increased our budget by some 300 per cent or 400 per cent to pay greater attention to the issues and concerns of farm women.
I do not want to leave the wrong impression here because we are fully aware of this. I think the Hon. Member will appreciate the fact that Agriculture Canada's responsibility, while recognizing this and trying to do something about it within its own shop, is really not the primary deliverers of programs of this kind. In fact, if one looked at some of the areas about which the Hon. Member talked, and they are shared, there is some federal responsibility. There is no question about it. If one examines the record one will see that the Government has responded in that particular area. However, a good number of them more appropriately fall within provincial jurisdiction. We do not have the facilities, the network, the people on the ground, or the extension people that provincial agricultural Departments have. There are reasons for this.
One must recognize what has happened in the past decade, or even less than a decade.
One has only to examine in detail the majority of cases that are going through the farm debt review process to find that almost without exception they fall into one category. That category includes those people who were told certain things and advised to do certain things in the early 1970s, because

May 9, 1988
Supply
certain things were going to happen in the 1980s. They took that advice. They did those things. They expanded their operations very dramatically. Then, of course, they were hit by 24 per cent interest rates and had to refinance. Some of those people are able to get through with some real difficulties.
But people who are in the grains and oilseeds sector are the ones who unfortunately are not able to get through. These are really days of paradox in Canadian agriculture. There has been record farm income in 1986 and 1987. Record farm income is being predicted for this year, 1988. This would not be the case if it had not been for the support programs provided to Canadian farmers by the Canadian Government.
From an agricultural point of view nothing is perfect. However, the record will stand the test of time. We delivered on all our campaign commitments. We have increased the budget by 400 per cent. We have taken 585 initiatives, delivering more than $9 billion, most of which has gone out in the form of direct farm support.
After having said that, I would not want anyone either in the agricultural community or anyone in Canada for that matter to think that this Minister of Agriculture, my cabinet colleagues and my caucus colleagues are not very much aware of the stress mentioned by the Hon. Member. We are going to try to do everything we can not only to minimize it but, hopefully, to eliminate it completely.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments of the Minister. A great many of these matters fall within provincial jurisdiction, especially in terms of social services, health, and so on. It might be worth while for the Minister to consider putting this item on the agenda for the next meeting he has with provincial Ministers of Agriculture. I am not sure when that is. I believe it is in July. They will be discussing the general problems facing farmers across the country. There might be some value in pursuing this item at a special conference. I do not want there to be a big study done, something which will delay things and cost all kinds of money. However, it may be worth while to have it as an agenda item and perhaps to have a working group from the federal and provincial ministers' conference to take a look at farm stress.
It is particularly important on the Prairies, as the Minister has said. In the grains and oilseeds sector there is a world crisis. That has been compounded by the fact that there is a drought. I am just thinking on my feet as we go along. I had not thought of this until the Minister got up. Perhaps it can be considered as an agenda item or for a working group to consider. It can offer some hope in this particular area. It can, if nothing else, co-ordinate the approach among the provinces.
The Minister mentioned one thing that is really important, which is the emotional weight falling on the shoulders of the farm woman. The study conducted by the Government of Saskatchewan stated that there is now an increase in abuse of the farm wife and an increase in the abuse of children. The
report states: "According to one special counsellor there is an increase in wife and child abuse, including sexual abuse, but also non-sexual abuse". Obviously the load falls more heavily on the unsung hero who is the farm woman. Over the years the farm woman has made a tremendous contribution not only to rural Canada but to Canada in terms of doing more than her fair share of the work on the farm and of making it a productive unit. She is the person who often receives no wage, no pension plan, and does not have the social net that many women working outside the farm and outside the home would have in an urban setting.
Or, had her total salary go into the farm.

Yes, or have her total salary go into the farm operation. Even in the best of times, the role played by the farm woman is a very difficult role and must be a very stressful role.
I grew up on a farm. I left the farm and went to university in the city. I know many farmers in my own riding, and in my community over the years since I was a small child. I know the contribution made by many of the women during those days. Even in the better days, in the 1950s and 1960s, and the booming agriculture days in western Canada in the 1970s, there was still an extra burden borne by farm women. Today they have this type of stress. I can think of examples in my riding where the male farmer is horrendously depressed by of things he cannot control by his own hands or brain in terms of his own operation because of trade wars or the rain does not fall, and in many ways the burden is even greater on that farmer's wife.
I wish to underline what the Minister has stated, but perhaps he could consider the possibility of this being an agenda item at the conference.

The program has also been made more flexible. Farmers can now opt for 60, 70 or 80 per cent coverage in some provinces. Since 1973, enrollment in federal-provincial crop insurance plans has increased significantly. Last year, almost 135,000 farmers participated in the Crop Insurance Program. More than 42 million acres were covered by insurance, with the federal Government contributing more than $180 million to crop insurance schemes across the country. Of that amount, more than $145 million was provided to western Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the Crop insurance officials are well aware of the dry conditions in much of western Canada. They well remember what happened in 1984, and again in 1985. This year, those officials have made a special effort to encourage farmers in the West to enroll in insurance plans. The deadlines for applications for crop insurance were widely publicized, and especially so in western Canada. Farmers had until the end of March to apply for coverage for forage and feed crops, and until the end of April for annual crops.
Estimates for this year indicate that more than 95,000 farmers from the prairie provinces will be covered by the Crop Insurance Program, with the breakdown being as follows: 16,800 farmers in Manitoba; 48,000 in Saskatchewan; and 30,500 in Alberta. Almost 3,000 farmers in British Columbia are expected to be covered.
The federal Government is pleased by the response of the producers. We are especially pleased that the registration of forage producers is up about 60 per cent, and that they have purchased 130 per cent more protection.
The federal-provincial crop insurance scheme has a proven track record. It is a vital part of the federal strategy, a strategy that very much addresses the concerns of the motion now being debated by this House. Crop insurance is in fact one long-term response of the federal Government to help protect Canadian producers against environmental disasters.
This Government is committed to crop insurance as the best means available to protect against crop loss. With crop insurance, farmers can be confident that they are well protected against the whims of nature-and that, Mr. Speaker, is what we are discussing this morning.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On questions and comments, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo).

Mr. Speaker, I have both a comment and a question in respect of crop insurance.
As I am sure the Hon. Member is aware, one of the concerns with having insurance as a long-term tool is that we eventually stabilize at a lower level as a result of a continuing reduction in production levels. That is a concern of those farmers who have experienced lower and lower production levels over a period of three or four years. Farmers in that circumstance are now at a point where they are insuring at a
level at which it no longer becomes worth while buying insurance.
In my region of Saskatchewan, the return on crops has dropped to a level where the insurance pay-out is not sufficient to pay one's production costs. That is a weakness of the Crop Insurance Program that is making itself felt in respect of a number of agricultural products.
I am wondering whether the Hon. Member has any suggestions to offer to federal-provincial crop insurance officials in respect of the problem of insurance levels dropping to the point where they no longer return even the cost of production to the producer.

I appreciate the comment and the question from the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo). Certainly I am aware of the ongoing discussions aimed at making the Crop Insurance Program as lucrative as possible for the producer. The program itself is designed to insure against disasters of nature, providing for those who suffer from such a disaster a return close to the average that would have been realized in normal circumstances.
I hope that the Hon. Member for Prince Albert is not confusing the 5-year averages with the stabilization program, something about which we all have a concern in respect of the development of averages. Certainly in my area of the country, regional averages have not been dramatically adjusted as a result of natural disasters impacting on crops. While we are now facing average lower incomes as a result of market prices, yield averages have not been drastically affected, to my knowledge.
Individual production records are carefully maintained by the crop insurance officials and individual producers can develop their own averages, based upon their own pattern of production, with the result that an individual producer, in the event of a disaster, can realize a return that reflects that producer's past yield pattern. Certainly, this is the case in my area of the country, and I am sure that it is not very much different in the western part of Canada to which the Hon. Member for Prince Albert referred.
I agree that we should try to do whatever we can to make the crop insurance plan as workable and as lucrative as possible for the producer. We need to have ongoing efforts aimed at encouraging producer participation.
The crop insurance plan is there for a purpose, and it is achieving its purpose. That is not to say it cannot be improved. Every system can stand improvement, and certainly we encourage efforts toward that end.

subsubtopic: THE HOMELESS-GOVERNMENT RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a recent press release from the office of the Public Works Minister (Mr. Mclnnes) announced that the sale of federal property had yielded over $170 million.
The purpose of this program was to reduce the number of surplus federal properties and to help bring down the federal deficit.
We would have hoped, Mr. Speaker, that the Conservative Government would take this opportunity to ensure that some of these spaces and buildings were converted into housing for Canada's 100,000 homeless.
On reading this press release, I noticed that several properties will be developed by private consortiums. For example, the Canlands in Ottawa will become an administrative complex; an old office building in Vancouver will be transformed into chic retail spaces; the RCMP building in Westmount will be replaced with twin towers for luxury housing; Dufferin Street in Toronto will be used for an industrial development and office building project. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the homeless have no voice in this House. The Minister has forgotten them.
On their behalf, I accuse the Minister of lack of leadership in this issue.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the students and faculty of John Abbott College of Ste. Anne de Bellevue, Quebec, for having recently declared their school a nuclear weapons free zone.
The effort to establish a nuclear weapons free zone at John Abbott was spearheaded by the Students Against Global Extermination, SAGE. They are justifiably proud of their important achievement. In their letter to me the students wrote:
We hope that in our act and the acts of groups like ourselves, in communities across Canada and the world, we will demonstrate that ordinary citizens will not tolerate the nuclear arm's race any further.
Their declaration is not simply a symbolic gesture. Rather, it is tangible evidence of a clear and compelling message that many Canadians share, that continued nuclear deployments, expansions, and modernizations are untenable and unacceptable.

RIGHT TO LIFE OF UNBORN CHILDREN Mr. Gordon Taylor (Bow River): Mr. Speaker:
Why is there always such a controversy over when life begins? Even if there is doubt that it is a human being from conception, what gives one the right to take that life? Am I free to shoot a rifle at an object if I am not certain what it is, especially if it might be a human being? The doubt must give that little unborn child a right to life that is equal to that of the mother. If there is not a human being at conception, at some point the fertilized ovum becomes one. If I had difficulty in believing that human life began at conception, I certainly would not want to be in the position of deciding whether it began at eight days, one month, three months or at birth. Anyone who claims to do that is taking the place of God.
This quotation came to me from Rev. Father Ken Forster of Fort St. James, B.C.
I believe that life begins at conception. When we write an abortion law, let us make sure it is based on the truth that the unborn have the right to live.

May 9, 1988
lives of 248 U.S. servicemen in Gander, Newfoundland, in December, 1985.
Members of the ground crew who worked on the ill-fated DC-8 prior to its fatal crash stated over the past weekend that "there was no ice build-up whatsoever on the aircraft prior to takeoff'.

Lives have been lost, Mr. Speaker. We have to make sure it is our responsibility that this tragic incident is not repeated. We can only do that with the facts.

subtopic: ELIMINATION OF EXEMPTION FOR CHILDREN 18 YEARS OR OLDER
ELIMINATION OF EXEMPTION FOR CHILDREN 18 YEARS OR OLDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under stage one of tax reform, parents of healthy children 18 years or older who live at home lose the current personal exemption of $1,200. A tax credit of $850 is offered for handicapped children. There is also a tax credit for post-secondary education tuition fees, but an 18-year-old still attending high school is not eligible, and in Ontario most grade 13 students are 18.
Single parents are hit hard. A single parent who formerly claimed the equivalent to married deduction for a dependent child over 18, valued at $3,740, can no longer do so. Imagine the financial burden being placed on a single person with a child over 18 still at home, either in high school or unemployed. Family allowance payments have stopped, support payments for the child from the other spouse have more than likely stopped, and now there is no tax relief.
In November of 1987 the Finance Committee recommended that the Government reconsider these proposals, but the Government has decided against it. The high cost to parents of supporting 18-year-olds should not have been ignored by the Government.

Mr. Speaker, a shameful incident occurred in Moncton, New Brunswick, during a demonstration organized by labour union leader Greg Murphy, a former NDP candidate. The wife of Canada's Prime Minister was insulted and attacked, and several children were injured. The demonstrators acted in a way that was degrading and harmful to the image of this country. In its Saturday edition, the Moncton Times reported that representatives of the federal NDP in Moncton had urged people to join the demonstration organized for that day.
The newspaper's report read as follows: "The Moncton wing of the federal NDP gave its unanimous support to a public demonstration organized to coincide with today's visit to Moncton by Prime Minister Mulroney".
I hope the Leader of the NDP will make a public statement to the Members of his Party and all those who contributed to this show of violence, and tell them that this kind of behaviour is anti-democratic and unacceptable for any political party in
this country. We were familiar with the verbal violence of Shirley Carr and Bob White, the labour leaders who are in bed with the NDP. But now, with organizers like Murphy, we have seen physical violence in Moncton!

Mr. Speaker, the backing down by the Government last week on film distribution policy was another cave-in on our independent cultural policy, and it is certainly not the last as a result of the influence of the free trade deal. Listen to what Jack McAndrew of Video Atlantic has to say about it:
Flora's bill has about as many teeth as one of my chickens-and they have more heart.
Not only will Canadian distributors be required to bid against Americans with more resources; the Americans can use their clout in controlling the American market to force the addition of Canadian rights to U.S. rights. It simply means more paperwork in signing two contracts instead of one. Flora's distribution fund won't do much in the face of that economic power.
We are seeing the first cultural casualty of the Free Trade Agreement.
The Americans squawk like a rooster in heat, and the Tories furiously lay another egg-a cracked egg.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal dominated other place has placed politics above the Canadian people by allowing the immigration system to become a world-class joke. Without passage of Bill C-55 and Bill C-84, Canada has to contend with the present inefficient and slow-moving refugee process.
The criminal element has seized this opportunity to escape prosecution in their own countries. Recently an American wanted for murder was using our liberal immigration law, which was passed by a Liberal Government, to thwart his return to the U.S. by claiming refugee status.
Our refugee laws are only to be applied to those who meet the UN definition of convention refugees. Criminals are exempt from these regulations. Only genuine refugees and the Canadian people are being hurt by the Liberal Senate's lack of responsibility.
