subsubtopic: ALLEGED COLLUSION IN REAL ESTATE INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
It has been reported that, for the past year, the Bureau of Competition Policy has been investigating concerns over collusion in some areas of the real estate industry, which collusion has been costing Canadian consumers many millions of dollars.
Can the Minister confirm that that investigation is actually going on, and whether or not some evidence of collusion has turned up; and if so, tell us what he intends to do about it?
Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Consumer and Corporate
Affairs): The Hon. Member is correct, the Bureau of Competition Policy has indeed been investigating the commission structure within the real estate industry. Some months ago, in fact, the Office of the Bureau of Competition Policy had cause to gather evidence from a number of real estate boards across the country, and that information is now being looked at.
Because of the distance that has to be maintained between my office and that of the Director of Investigation and Research, I am unable, under law, to know precisely where that investigation now rests. I am told that it is being pursued with dispatch and that some recommendation will be made in the near future. Whether the decision will be to lay charges, I cannot say at this point in time.

By way of supplementary, is the Minister advising us that there are weaknesses in the law? And if there are weaknesses in the law, does the Minister intend to change the law; and if so, when does he propose to do so?
If the investigation indicates that there has been a contravention of the law, and no charges are laid, one has to ask why the law is not being applied.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not prepared to conclude that there are weaknesses in the law. In fact, the new competition law, passed by this House in June of 1986, has shown itself to be a very useful tool in ensuring competition in a wide variety of areas. I would be pleased to go over with the Hon. Member the successes that have been achieved in this regard.
The investigation in question is a trans-Canada one, involving many jurisdictions. It is quite complex.
May 9, 1988

The Director of Investigation and Research is pursuing the investigation with dispatch, and I have total confidence in his ability. I am sure he will reach the proper conclusion in the near future.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the same Minister and is on the same subject.
I respect the fact that the Minister has to keep a distance between himself and the Bureau of Competition Policy. However, recently a spokesman for the Bureau of Competition Policy made the statement that the Government simply cannot lower commission rates.
My question for the Minister is this. Does he agree with that statement?
Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Consumer and Corporate
Affairs): In a general sense, yes, since there is no ability on the part of my Department, in any one of its branches, either to increase prices or lower prices from where they are. However, if in fact there are anti-competitive aspects involved, aspects that are contrary to the Competition Act, and those are removed, I have every confidence that competition in the marketplace would cause a lowering of rates. That is the objective. Certainly we cannot lower rates by fiat or direction. It is only through increasing competition that we can bring about a lowering of rates.

The
Minister knows that the Competition Act makes it illegal for anyone to conspire to fix prices or to lessen competition, whether in sales or in services.
Will the Minister intervene in support of the Canadian consumer? Or is the Minister willing to let the case go to court?
Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Consumer and Corporate
Affairs): I await the recommendation of the Director of Investigation and Research in respect of whether in fact there is evidence of collusion to fix prices and whether a successful prosecution could result.
More important, what I am after is to try to ensure that there is as much competition as possible in the marketplace, since I believe that that is the way the consumer will get the greatest benefit.
There was cause to be suspicious in this situation, and that is why the investigation was launched. But, in fairness, I have to await the results of the investigation before reaching any conclusion as to culpability, or otherwise, on the part of any of the participants.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: TOBACCO FARMERS-PAYMENTS UNDER REDUX PROGRAM
speechtext:

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Althouse:
That this House urge the government to provide for emergency financial assistance to grain and livestock producers in the southern Prairies and in Central British Columbia in the event of a continuation of the current drought conditions in those areas, and to establish a long-term plan to deal with environmental disasters such as droughts, floods, and pest infestations.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take this opportunity to say a few words on the motion my colleague has put before the House. Farming these days in most parts of Canada is not a particularly happy industry. The attack on farming has come not only from nature but from a variety of other sources as well. It has not
Supply
been caused by drought, floods, insects or disease necessarily, but by many artificial sources including ourselves and other Governments in the world which are attempting to control the market.
A part of the difficulty with farming is caused by world events, world markets, low prices, price wars, and unfair subsidies. However, it is because of this rather unstable situation in which farmers find themselves, while attempting to produce the food the world needs, that we have before us a motion which suggests that we need to do something about stability in farming.
What farmers really need is some kind of long-term security. They need to know that what they plant and the animals they nurture will provide a return sufficient to pay the bills and to make a little profit so that they can have a decent life for themselves and their families. They need enough to make sure that they will stay alive, not only in the sense of having enough to eat, but in the industry they have chosen for themselves.
Prices and markets are artificial difficulties which farmers face. We are asking in this motion why we do not have in place a program which gives farmers some assurance that when they hit a bad year, when they are affected by those difficulties which nature sometimes throws up, they will have a program which allows other Canadians to be of support to farmers.
Back in 1985 the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) came before this House and made a very specific statement. This was during a time when there was a considerable amount of concern about drought in southern Saskatchewan. The Government acted on that concern and put in the works a considerable amount of money to assist farmers. It was a rather temporary approach, as the Minister said at the time. On November 27, 1985, at page 8870 of Hansard, he said:
There is no question about the fact that there are many western farmers, good farmers, who, through no fault of their own, need special assistance measures at this time.
That is what he was providing; that was the announcement. He went on:
But we all appreciate that ad hoc measures and programs are not an ideal solution. It is disruptive to producers to live with the uncertainty of not knowing what back-up assistance they will receive when natural disasters occur.
He went on to say:
Nor is it easy for the federal Government to take on substantial new financial commitments which have not been previously budgeted.
Yet what the Government has been doing ever since is coming up with ad hoc programs when farmers need assistance. We are suggesting today that it is time that the Government looked for a program which will guarantee farmers that if they face natural disasters they can at least know-and that is the key-that there are programs in place which will help them in the circumstances.

May 9, 1988
Supply
Farming is a difficult business. Drought, floods, grasshoppers, disease, and bad weather are all disasters confronting farmers much more often than possibly we realize because we have a tendency to look at these things as they affect only our little area. They may not bother us too much because we may be affected by only one of them every few years. If we were to put in place a regularized structure, a disaster relief program, then the farmer would know that he or she would receive enough to live on in case of a disaster.
We can look at what has happened in Canada over the years. We have had tornadoes, floods, and other natural disasters, and I suppose in every case the Government has come forward with enough to allow the farmers to survive through the particular problem. The Minister and other Members of the House have suggested that crop insurance is now the solution to all such disasters. Perhaps under certain circumstances it is. Others have suggested that western grain stabilization or that kind of program is also an answer. Again I say maybe, but it is not always the answer. Farmers know that both those programs are based on historical production. The farmer's income is stabilized at a level which is the average of several years before.
Today, as well, several Hon. Members have said that right now we are faced on parts of the Prairies with the same kind of weather patterns we had in the Dirty Thirties. In fact, they have used those particular words, "the Dirty Thirties". One of the features of the Dirty Thirties was that the problems lasted for a good portion of the years between 1930 and 1938.
The Saskatoon Star Phoenix carried a little item this weekend entitled "Fifty years ago today, historical note". It said that 50 years ago today the Province of Saskatchewan received two inches of rain. It was the first general rainfall Saskatchewan had had for eight years. I am not being pessimistic and suggesting that that is what will happen now, but we have no emergency funding for such a long-term disaster. Insurance programs do not deal with such situations.
In fact, when the Minister made his comments on November 27, 1985, he pointed out to this House that one particular portion of the agricultural industry, the cattle raising industry, had had five continuous years of insufficient pasture. Stabilization programs do not help in such circumstances. The programs about which we have been talking will provide shortterm relief, as the Minister said in a press release at that time.
Speaking about the program for drought in western Canada, as well as crop insurance and western grain stabilization, he said that this program would provide short-term relief while we developed a long-term approach to emergency funding. He explained that the Crop Disaster Assistance Program was being viewed as a field test for a permanent emergency assistance program which would be an adjunct to the current Crop Insurance Program. He said that in the past few months it had been referred to as "Phase 3" of the drought assistance
plan. The Minister of Agriculture indicated this in a wire released early in 1986. He was pointing to the need for a longterm program which takes care of natural disasters as they come about.
The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) keyed in on one of the results of not having in place programs which allow farmers to believe that when they plant they can harvest, that when they breed cattle they will be able to live off the products of those cattle. If, when in the process of planting or of raising cattle, you never know whether the results of your year's work will be enough to keep you and your family alive for the next year, you are under a tremendous amount of stress.
The aim of our motion today is to draw the attention of the Government and the people of Canada to the fact that there is a great deal of pressure on farmers these days due to the fact that they do not get sufficient return on their products to allow them to live, to pay their accumulated debts, and to pay the input necessary to produce the products they wish to market.
One of the results of this in many areas of the country has been an effect on the rural population which Members of this House and citizens of Canada abhor. There has been an increased number of family problems in the rural areas- increased alcoholism, suicides, drug use, and emotional problems. These are all much more prevalent in rural areas now than ever before. Not too long ago a statistic in Ontario suggested that more than one-third of the deaths in its rural areas were by suicide, related in most cases to inability to deal with the problems of farm production.
We are, therefore, suggesting today that it may be possible to eliminate some of the stress by putting in place an income security program based on the farmer as an important and integral part of society, because the farmer is an important and integral part of society. The only link in the food chain from the resource earth to the consumer which does not pay for itself is the producer, the farmer. The only link in the chain which does not make enough from the day-to-day work to pay itself a decent living, to pay for products and input, is the actual producer.	,
I have been talking about the need to eliminate as much of the stress of farmers as possible. The drought may disappear. It could rain tomorrow. However, we have a water shortage and that will not disappear tomorrow. A flood starts today and remains for a few days. A drought which causes water shortage does not happen overnight; it is built up over years. In western Canada the water shortage has been developing for many years, and it is not going to disappear.
Therefore we need not only expand the very successful and worth-while projects which PFRA has in place. We need to put in place a disaster program which will eliminate at least one of the causes of the great amount of stress put on the farmer as he tries to make a living.
May 9, 1988

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have one short comment. I certainly recognize the seriousness of the drought problem in the Prairies which at this time particularly relates to water for the livestock operations. In the area I represent, the PFRA is working. It is pumping water into dugouts in community pastures, trying to make water available in as many cases as is possible so that there is drinking water for the livestock.
Another comment I would like to make is that having been the chairman of the task force on drought back in 1984-85, I can say that the Government did respond very positively. The positive news we have on the Prairies, as reported by the CBC this morning, is that approximately one-third of Saskatchewan has received sufficient rainfall, along with a better part of Manitoba. The drought area certainly lies in the western and central parts of the province. On a positive note, the Government has been responsive and I am sure will be responsive to these needs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
In reply to the comments of the Hon. Member, I will say that all of us who live in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, recognize the great value of the PFRA programs now and in the past. The PFRA was established for a good reason in the 1930s and the fact it has survived is a good indication that it has done a job and done it well. As far as water is concerned, based on the precipitation in Saskatchewan right now, there are parts of Saskatchewan that will have no problem, but there are parts which will be in trouble. Estevan, for example, has had 40 per cent of normal precipitation up until now. The chance it will reach normal precipitation levels by the end of June is only 24 per cent. In other words, there is one chance out of four that Estevan will have normal precipitation this year. I will go through the statistics very quickly. They are a good indication of how badly things are with respect to water on the Prairies. The statistics are only for Saskatchewan. There is only one chance out of three that Saskatoon will have enough rainfall by June 30 to be up to normal levels of precipitation. Prince Albert has 61 per cent of normal precipitation. It is by far the best in the area. Battleford has 29 per cent, Broadview, 27 per cent, Yorkton, 29 per cent, Estevan, 24 per cent, Regina, 34 per cent and Swift Current, 27 per cent.
Those percentages are indications that we may get some rain, but we need a considerable amount more. That is only part of our motion here today. The main part of our motion says we need in place something which can cushion the farmer so that he knows for sure he going to survive. I appreciate the point the Hon. Member made, that the Government has reacted in the past to give farmers assistance when they needed it, but it would be much less stressful for the farmer if a program was in place that was regularized and structured.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do wish to comment and put a question to the Hon. Member for Prince Albert. I found his speech a bit confusing as I listened. He went through his points one by one. He began to deal with a motion for a strategy to
Supply
deal with environmental disasters, but he tried to couple that with the problem many farmers face with respect to low commodity prices from time to time, particularly during the past two years when we have been dealing with the Special Grains Assistance Program and so on. I find it difficult to lump these two problems together. Why is the Hon. Member attempting to deal with the motion and at the same time trying to deal with low commodity prices? It appears as if he is attempting to deal with a type of insurance plan to cover both at the same time.
I also want to point out that we recognize that the crop insurance program is not perfect, but the Hon. Member seems not to be aware of how it is set up. Surely he knows that the individual farmer starts off on the program with a regional average as a basis to be paid in case he faces some type of disaster and does not harvest his crop, but as he participates in the program, the Hon. Member will know that each farmer has the opportunity to develop his own personal record of production, thereby increasing the level at which he would be paid in case he faces a disaster.
The Hon. Member is confusing that program with the stabilization program, and they must not be confused because it just confuses everyone who listens to the Hon. Member. So let us deal with environmental problems, and the disasters with respect to those environmental problems, such as grasshoppers, floods, droughts, and, as I pointed out previously, some of the frost problems. I would ask the Hon. Member if he would agree that we have to deal with those issues independently. Surely he knows the Government has a record of being there with special disaster funds, besides the insurance programs, and so on.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps we did not make our motion broad enough. Disasters are the same whether they come about from low prices or from no rain. They are all a disaster when it comes to getting bread on the table. I want to point out that historically in my part of Saskatchewan, and the Hon. Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) will recognize this, the use of insurance to cover crops is not very broadly used because we in my particular district have never been able to establish a level which would allow us to make use of the insurance program. I recognize the difference without any doubt between insurance and stabilization, but historically the two somehow seem to come together in our part of Saskatchewan because of the fact that by the time the farmer has paid the amount necessary for input and insured the crop at that level, he has already used up any possible returns he might get from insurance. Consequently, most farmers do not bother to buy insurance. It is only of marginal value to some people.
The other point I think I have to make is that when a farmer is under stress, when he is having a problem making ends meet, one of the things he has a tendency to drop is insurance, just as many people dropped Western Grain Stabilization when they should not have. It is that stress that builds up which causes the problems of alcoholism, suicide and family problems.

May 9, 1988
Supply
Stress causes the kinds of problems which some kind of a program that guaranteed a return under certain circumstances would eliminate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have one short supplementary comment to make. The NDP in Saskatchewan has been opposed to the building of a dam called Rafferty Dam at Estevan, Saskatchewan. The Elon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Elovdebo) mentioned Estevan and the low rainfall in that area.
The Devine Government is moving ahead on this dam which will have a very positive effect on water supply in the whole southern area. Yet the NDP has taken the position of opposing this structure. Certainly, the building of dams for water supply has to be a very positive aspect. The Rafferty Dam is a very positive direction that the provincial Government has taken with the assistance of the federal Government.
There seems to be somewhat of a contradiction here in the NDP line in terms of suggesting on the one hand that we have to look at water supplies and then on the other hand putting road-blocks in the way of the provincial Government accomplishing the building of dams. Someone said that the NDP in Saskatchewan talks about dams and the Conservatives build them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Rafferty Dam in Saskatchewan is a political dam. It has nothing to do with water particularly. It is a political dam which is being put in place for the benefit of the Hon. Member. It will take 35 years to fill the dam, if it can ever be filled up. If the water level in the dam is dropped by one metre there will be 60 miles of mudflats. This information has come out of a partially developed study which the Government of Saskatchewan never bothered to finish. It got the people to do the study with respect to this particular dam development and did not fill in the blanks that were necessary to make a decision on the building of the dam or the not building of it, which has nothing to do with the economy, water use or anything else about that particular area.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to enter into the debate which is, of course, of very considerable importance to the agricultural community in western Canada. In doing so I speak at least in part from my own perspective as a Manitoban. I might say that, unfortunately, some of my colleagues who I know wish to be here cannot be present today. I think in particular of the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer) who could not be present.
I am pleased to report to the House that the situation in Manitoba has changed rather dramatically in the last 10 days. Rather ironically while all of us shared the concern about an impending and feared drought in western Canada some 10 to 14 days ago, in Manitoba we now have a situation of having to look at damage caused by flooding in the northwestern part of
Manitoba in the Dauphin-Swan River area. I suppose this simply demonstrates how quickly weather conditions can change. In a sense we can go from one crisis to another.
The rains of the last two weeks have moved the area of concern to the West. I am advised that at least the eastern third of Saskatchewan has had enough moisture that it can look to reasonable chances of germination. That, of course, is good news. The problem for cattlemen and livestock producers remains since their water needs will not be met as readily as those who are involved in cereal grains.
If I may, I want to make some reference to the exchange that took place in the House a few moments ago with respect to the Rafferty Dam. So much of what happens in Canada depends on one's geographic perspective. In light of the fact that I represent the constituency of Brandon-Souris, and since the Souris River flows from Saskatchewan into North Dakota and back into Manitoba, I must advise my hon. friend, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Gustafson), that there are as yet some unresolved concerns in my own constituency with respect to water supply. I simply say to him for the sake of the record that if I understand it correctly, the role of the federal Government is limited to that of providing its permission for construction to proceed. If I understand correctly, I think that that is still under review.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Member who just spoke on behalf of the New Democratic Party, a good friend of mine of several years standing, said that what western Canadian farmers want to a very large degree is an assurance that they can count on the federal Government to be of assistance if indeed the need for that assistance proves to be there. While all of us in the House understand how quickly weather conditions can change on the Prairies, the drought that we fear today could indeed be gone in 48 hours. Thus we do understand the importance of the concerns which are there.
We want to take this opportunity to reassure the prairie agricultural community, although it understands full well, that the Government has been there in the past when it was needed since 1984. I think the community understands full well that we will be there again if indeed our assistance is necessary.
I am pleased that there have been some changes to western grain stabilization programs and crop insurance, which have made them more responsive to the needs of prairie agriculture. For example, we now have provisions for livestock feed forage crops to be included under crop insurance to a greater degree than they were before. While I, like other Members, appreciate the need for long-term planning, it is very difficult in some instances to have the kind of long-term planning which some of us would seek. That is particularly true when talking about drought.
Part of the problem with drought is the fact that it does not necessarily follow a uniform pattern. For example, I think of programs which the federal Government put in place in 1984
May 9, 1988

and 1985 in which the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister played a very significant role. I remember some $60 million was provided in 1984. I believe that something in the order of $146 million was provided in 1985. I remember one of the problems at that particular time was the fact that for those programs to proceed there had to be provincial co-operation as well. Due perhaps to variations in economic conditions, and perhaps due to the attitudes of provincial Governments, some of the farmers in my own constituency were not able to participate in the latter program because the Government of Manitoba did not believe the crisis was as severe as the federal Government believed it was. Our neighbours to the west in Saskatchewan and Alberta were able to participate in those programs, and benefit from them.
As you may know, Mr. Speaker, the new Government of Manitoba was sworn in this afternoon. There is as of now a new Minister of Agriculture. I am sure that that new Minister of Agriculture will be very responsive and sensitive to the needs of the agricultural community, I believe to a greater degree than has been the case over the last few years. What the farm community understandably seeks, and what we as the Government are prepared to offer, is a statement of commitment on our part. One might well ask in view of the cynicism which exists among the public today just how the farm community is to determine that a Government's commitment is something which indeed will be honoured.
We as politicians live in a world of words. In fact, the very word "parliament" means "to speak". There are many who would suggest that there is far too much speaking that goes on in Parliament. I think there are some of us who would applaud that.If we cannot judge a Government or politicians by their words, the obvious question arises as to how does one judge a Government. How do we know that it will honour its commitments?
As a Member of the Government, and particularly as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture, I am pleased to be able to say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the prairie agricultural community that I believe this Government's commitment to the agricultural community will be respected and well received, not because of the words which we use here or elsewhere, but because of the actions which have preceded the words and the actions of the last four years.
I have no difficulty in saying that the crisis which has existed in agriculture for the past four or five years has been the worst that we have seen in Canada since the 1930s. I also have no hesitation in saying to the Canadian agricultural community that the record of the Government over the past four years is one of unprecedented support for agriculture. Nowhere in the history of Canada has there been a four year period of growing financial support for agriculture as there has been for the past four years. The strength of our commitment is to be measured and determined by that record of which I speak.
Supply
I have referred to the fact that when there was a drought in 1984 and in 1985, programs were put in place which met the needs of the agricultural community. We have also moved to try to strengthen the safety net programs to which we as government Members refer. I have mentioned amendments to the Western Grains Stabilization Act, amendments to crop insurance, and other Members have previously spoken on that.
We live so much in the age of dollars and cents that sometimes our record is measured only in those terms. Perhaps one statistic alone is more significant than any other, that is, our direct financial support to Canadian agriculture has increased by some 400 per cent since 1984. That is an unprecedented record of increased financial assistance to agriculture. That is why the farmers realize that when we say we will be there, we will indeed be there.
However, many of the problems which exist in agriculture today are not of a short-term nature, but of a long-term nature. Many are international in nature, rather than national or regional. That is why the Government has worked very hard to address these problems at the international level. That is why agriculture has been more on the international agenda than ever before in the history of Canada.
In June, 1986, Canada hosted a meeting of five major grain exporters to work toward solutions and problems in the grain trade. In September, 1986, there was a very important development when the Secretary of State participated in the launching of a new GATT round. We understand very clearly that GATT was tragically ignored in the last talks by the previous administration. Agriculture is on the GATT round for the first time. Much is expected of that, but indeed I think there is reason to be optimistic about what is expected.
In May, 1987, Canada and the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds played an integral part in the meeting of the Cairns Group, a group of 14 nations that are among the principal grain exporters moving toward trade reforms. In a similar fashion, at the economic summits, and at the OECD meetings, agriculture has been very much on the agenda as a result of initiatives that we have taken.
In addition, we have had a considerable amount of success in moving grain under very competitive circumstances. We have used short and medium term credit measures through the Export Development Corporation to facilitate those sales. We have had agricultural trade missions to Japan, the Soviet Union, and China. We signed a five year commitment with the Soviet Union, which continues to be a very important economic trading partner. As a result of that commitment, the Soviet Union has agreed to purchase a minimum 25 million tonnes of grain. There is a new three year agreement with Brazil. As a result of these various activities, the total representing last year was a record export of 31 million tonnes. This has been done at a time when some of our competitors have been attempting to give away their grain in order to take away markets that have been historically ours. We have succeeded

not only in retaining our traditional markets, but adding to them.
At home we have done what we can to be of assistance. As I stated previously, we have done more than any other Government prior to us. For example, in October, 1984, although it is a long time ago in our memories, the St. Lawrence Seaway's tolls were frozen, saving farmers some $2 million. In January,
1985,	a moratorium was introduced on the Farm Credit Corporation foreclosures until the Farm Debt Review Boards were in place. As a result of the Farm Debt Review Boards being in place, and those many agricultural-minded citizens who work on them, we estimate that some 2,000 farmers remain in business today who would not otherwise be there. Funding for those boards has been extended until 1991 because the need is evident. There is a further federal commitment in that regard of $40 million.
In February, 1985 the Western Grain Stabilization Act was amended in order that farmers could receive interim payments in time for spring seeding. As a result of some of those amendments, and as a result of the support for the program, that program has paid out nearly $3.6 billion, $2.4 billion of that amount having been paid in the spring when it is needed most.
In June, 1985, and I remember this well because I was Chairman of the Agriculture Committee, we succeeded in establishing tripartite stabilization programs for red meat producers. Unfortunately, many provinces have not yet joined in the beef area, Manitoba being one of them, but I think that will come in the not too distant future.
In October, 1985, there were special cash advances of up to $3,000 per farmer to help prairie producers pay for the cost of drying grain. The problem at that time was too much moisture, the opposite of what it is now. In November, 1985 there were cash advances for unthreshed grain on the Prairies. The list goes on, Mr. Speaker.
There are federal tax rebates for farmers worth some $200 million per year at the moment. In March, 1986, there was a $94 million branch line rehabilitation program. In April, 1986, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced a freeze on the freight rates paid by producers for moving their grain. In July,
1986,	there was an investment of $35 million to promote the long term development of the livestock feed sector in Atlantic Canada. In December, 1986, there was the Special Canadian Grains Program, the first of two. The first was $1 billion, and more recently there was $1.1 billion in December, 1987.
In April, 1987, $64 million was provided to farmers to cushion them from a statutory increase in western grain freight rates. Presently there is another program of a lesser nature, but with the same objective. In December, 1987 assistance was given to the Farm Credit Corporation, recognizing that the credit crisis is not going to be resolved immediately. There was $30 million in extra funding provided in order that it could participate in lowering debts and interest rates with the Farm Debt Review Boards, and there is a promise of
$100 million per year for each of the next three years to permit them to do the same thing.
There was also an attempt to strengthen the FCCs. Last December $100 million was announced to cover corporate losses, and a deferral of a $103 million loan payment which lessened the crisis they were facing. Of course, there was also the extremely important $1.1 billion program to which I have already alluded.
Despite the fact that some $29 billion is being spent on interest on the national debt, the Government honoured the commitment it made some four years ago that farmers would be entitled to substantial capital gains tax exemptions. We recognize that the land they own and seek to pay for represents their own pension fund. Farmers are treated in the unique manner they deserve as a result of tax exemptions of some $500,000 per farmer.
In the past four years, as a result of all those programs and many to which I have not referred, our financial commitment to agriculture has risen by some 400 per cent, virtually 100 per cent per year for each of the four years we have been in power. This averages out to some $20,000 per year to each commercial farm in 1987, as contrasted with figures of some $4,000 per year in 1984.
Virtually every farmer to whom I speak, and there are many, would prefer that these types of programs were not necessary. They would prefer not to have to come to Government in times of stress. They would prefer that all of their necessary income could be found in the market-place. But agriculture is a very unique industry, in the sense that it depends entirely on the weather. I remember well living in Saskatchewan north of Regina in my teen years during the dry years when as a young person one spent more time looking at the sky than anything else, not to enjoy the beauty of the sky, but to look for rain clouds and worry about what agriculture could mean to prairie people who are so dependent upon the climate and the weather.
Agriculture is unique not only because it depends on the weather, but also because it depends, to a very large degree, on what international markets are. On the one hand, the Canadian farmer is historically very much of an individualist, but on the other hand he recognizes that he is in a uniquely dependent situation. I can think of no sector of the Canadian economy where those who practise that economy are as dependent on others as is the case in agriculture, and are particularly dependent upon forces over which there is no control. In my own constituency until 10 days ago the dirt and the dust was blowing, reminiscent of the 1940s and the 1930s. What is so tragic about that situation is there is very little that the individual farmer can do about that.
The farmer is in the same position when the price of grain declines. Who else in this society has suffered a 40 to 50 per cent reduction in the price for their product? That is what has
May 9, 1988

happened to the prairie grain producer over the last two, three, four years. Those are aspects of an agricultural operation which all of us regret, and they are aspects which we as a Government, in conjunction with our provincial counterparts, are striving to minimize to the greatest degree possible.
I wish it were possible for Members of this Government to stand in this Elouse today and say that there will be no drought in the Prairies. That, of course, is not possible. No one can accurately forecast what will happen with the weather. Certainly no one was forecasting the flooding which has taken place over the last few days in the Swan River Valley.
I wish we could stand in this place and outline precisely what we intend to do should the drought continue. But that, too, is difficult to do, given that we do not know the nature of the crisis as it will unfold. We do not know how large an area will be affected. What we do know is that we, as Members of this Government, can stand in this place and say to the prairie grain producers that we have been there over the last four years to an extent that no government before us has been there; and we can say to the prairie grain producers that we will not abandon them in their moment of need.
We have demonstrated our commitment to agriculture over the last four years a way of which I am personally proud, and we say to the agricultural community today that, if the need is there, we will be there again, as we were in 1984, as we were in 1985; that we will do whatever is necessary to assist the prairie agricultural community in the manner in which they deserve.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Clark), in his speech, spoke about certainty, and the difficulty that farmers have in feeling dependent. He should be aware that that is precisely the feeling that we are trying to address through this motion. The Government promised on November 27, 1985, in the Minister's statement, to continue its efforts toward developing a long-term approach to emergency funding. This motion is to remind the Government of that promise.
Until becoming a Member of this House, I depended upon farming as my sole source of livelihood, and I can tell the Hon. Member that farmers do not feel any sense of certainty from the kinds of statements that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister has made today. The farmers can take no certainty in being told that this Party, or that Party or the other Party will look after their interests. The sense of certainty that farmers are looking for is that which comes with a law, the kind of law that gave us, as farmers, the Western Grain Stabilization Administration. We got that because the law was there, not because a given party was in power. We got that because it was enacted as a law of the land.
That is the kind of certainty that farmers are looking for with regard to emergency drought aid. They want to know the parameters of the aid and what is required before action is triggered. They want to know what federal and provincial committees have to be put in place.
This all happens after the fact, and a formula is worked out. But, it is not enacted with any certainty. No one remembers from one emergency to the next what steps have to be gone through. It is something that has never been spelled out in the law. That is what we are trying to remind the Government of, since it seems to have forgotten what happened some three years ago on the occasion of the last emergency confronting the agricultural community.
Farmers want to know that the processes and steps are the same from one emergency to another, and they want them set out in the law. At the moment, those steps and procedures are

May 9, 1988
Supply
not set out in any orderly procedure, and there is no organization within any of the Departments to take over should we be in the middle of an election campaign at the time of a disaster, or going through a change of Government, or whatever.
Farmers must have the kind of certainty that can be had through having the steps and procedures set out in law, and that is what we are trying to stress through this particular motion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
: I appreciate the security which a law may provide-and I say that as someone whose own farm is still within the dry area of Saskatchewan. On the other hand, it may merely lend to a false sense of security, inasmuch as one cannot anticipate, in advance, all that the weather can do in terms of its impact upon the agricultural sector. One can simply not foresee all of the vagaries of weather.
In 1985, I had farmers in my own constituency, in the Grand Clairiere area, who suffered from drought, as well as from grasshoppers. Because those twin disasters were, so-called, local in nature, they could not qualify for assistance. The provincial government of the day took the position that the drought was not serious enough. My own inclination would be to proceed on an ad hoc basis, in belief that when one responds to the real circumstances of the moment, one can respond more adequately when trying to foresee the future.
There was no law which required the Government of Canada, in 1986, to provide a special $1 billion program to the Canadian agricultural community. Yet, because of the need, the Government responded with a $1 billion program. And there was no law which required the Government to respond in
1987.	Because the need was there, this Government did respond.
Those who believe that they can adequately prepare for the future through perfect legislation, legislation which encompasses all of the circumstances which the future will present, have a naive belief in the power of legislators to anticipate the future.

speechtext: The Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), on a question or comment.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have one or two comments and then I have a question for the Hon. Member. In my constituency, and probably in many parts of Alberta it is very, very dry. Last Saturday I dug down into the earth with my hands-I did not have a shovel-around eight or nine inches. The soil was bone dry. Hon. Members know that unless you have some moisture in the top four or five inches there is very little sense putting in seed because it will not germinate. There is a great deal of concern about this drought.
When I was in the Alberta Government, we explored plans for a catastrophe fund. People by themselves cannot provide for a catastrophe. You can provide for small happenings, but
you cannot provide for a catastrophe. We checked with Lloyds of London and others for a catastrophe insurance fund so that something could be in place when a tremendous flood or a devastating fire occurred, wiping out neighbourhoods, et cetera. These things may never happen but if there is a fund in place, it gives people a sense of security.
The United States has programs in place for emergencies. Frankly, I would like to see an expanded insurance policy or catastrophe fund, whatever you want to call it, set up. It may not look after every catastrophe or emergency that arises-no one can foresee everything, as the Parliamentary Secretary said. There is a feeling today that, sure, the Government will come through, but no one knows how, why or when a catastrophe will occur. If we do not get rains in Alberta in the next two or three weeks, it will be terrible for growth. Farmers will be unable to put in their seed. That will cause a calamity not only for Alberta but for Canada. We depend upon the farmers to produce our food.
Would the Parliamentary Secretary take a look at an expanded insurance policy or having a catastrophe fund-I do not care what it is called-in place that will give the farmer a feeling of security if the grasshoppers come in hordes, as they did in southern Alberta a year or two ago, when they destroyed crops and ate paint off the houses. We have no provision for those sorts of things, but something should be done in conjunction with provincial Governments. I would like to see the farmer given a feeling of security that if some of these terrible things happen and he cannot seed, he will not be left high and dry. This has been done in the United States. Canada can similarly set up a program. It will not cover everything but at least something would be there in the event of a catastrophe. I would like the comments of the Parliamentary Secretary.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) knows, there is a need for both levels of Government to work together to try to provide some sort of catastrophe fund, safety net or whatever. I would be the first to admit that perhaps there are too many programs but we have created a series of programs, both federal and provincial Governments working together. We have crop insurance, western grain stabilization and soil and water conservation programs. We have done many things. I would readily concede that there probably has not been as much coordination and integration of those as I would wish. We are spending a very substantial amount of money on agriculture on the Prairies, as the Hon. Member knows well. I referred to some of those figures in my address. We subsidize the movement of grain and there are various programs to keep down the farmer's share of freight rates, et cetera.
Part of the difficulty, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure the Hon. Member is aware and sensitive to this, is that while we believe that some of our programs are advantageous, the farmers do not necessarily agree. For a variety of reasons they choose not to participate. I think particularly of the Western Grain Stabilization Program which has paid out a substantial
May 9, 1988

amount of money to those who are in it. But what of the 13 per cent who are not in it? That is a problem this Elouse will have to address in the next few days or weeks.
There are people who would advocate that we could take the various programs, roll them together and probably provide to a substantial degree the sort of insurance coverage to which the Elon. Member refers. But what of the 40 per cent who do not choose to be in crop insurance for a variety of reasons? What about the 13 per cent who are not in the Western Grain Stabilization Program? Part of the difficulty in providing that kind of a safety net is that we are left with the understandable desire on the part of individual farmers to reserve the right to participate or not participate. That is why in some ways this special grains program, ad hoc though it may have been, was a response that met the needs of agriculture, I would argue quite well, because it was there. It was drafted after the circumstances were known. We knew what the situation was. We knew how far the price had fallen. We knew the size of the crop and the quality of the grain. We said in consultation with the farm communities that it was available to the community as a whole.
I have no lack of sympathy for the Elon. Member's objective in terms of trying to integrate these programs. But what do we do for those who for a variety of economic or philosophical reasons do not wish to participate?
Crop insurance is not nearly as adequate as it should be. For that reason many do not buy it. Many are buying it this year for the first time because of their concerns, but it is not adequate for many. The Western Grain Stabilization Program only covers a certain percentage of production. I would like to see us try to bring all this money together into a more comprehensive fund. But what about those who do not wish to participate? That remains a philosophical problem.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the environment critic for the New Democratic caucus, I am pleased to take part in this debate today because agriculture is extremely important to Canada and primary production is something highly dependent upon the environment. We are dealing with what we hope will be treated as a renewable resource. Far too often we see agriculture treated as a mining resource, as something that is here today and gone tomorrow. It is with a view to looking at agriculture as sustainable development that I participate in this debate and address some of the questions that my colleagues have already raised, specifically with regard to drought in western Canada, the need for long-term solutions and some security for our farmers.
It is a very discouraging prospect for us to consider the matter of drought in western Canada. We think of the drought in the 1930s and we are told that some of these scenes are beginning to happen again with sand, dust and soil blowing across the Prairies as they did at that time.
Droughts are not necessarily caused by some mysterious forces of nature over which we have no control. Droughts can be "man-made". Certainly human activities can influence the weather. The weather is not a given-that comes from the outside. What we do in terms of our forests and the renewal of the cycle of moisture in the air will be extremely important. We have to look to the possibility of the greenhouse effect which means carbon dioxide building up in the atmosphere, trapping heat close to the earth's surface, raising the temperature world-wide and as a result melting the polar caps and raising the level of the sea. One of the consequences of that can be the wiping out of populations along sea coasts. One of the other consequences, more pertinent to the debate before us today, is massive changes in weather and the possibility of drought on a permanent basis in areas that right now are very productive.
What are we doing about this? The Government has set up an international conference of the air. That is one of the things at which this conference will be looking at the end of June in Toronto. I applaud the initiative taken to bring countries

May 9, 1988
Supply
together to look at these basic, long-term potential environmental disasters.
What are we doing in the meantime? We continue to burn fossil fuels. We are becoming ever more dependent on them, and part of the policy of the Government is to increase this dependence. Under the trade deal, there will be an even faster use of our fossil fuels. Fossil fuels are major sources of the carbon dioxide that causes the greenhouse effect.
Rain forests in South America are being destroyed. We are not directly involved in that destruction as we are not there in person, cutting down rain forests, but we are part of a worldwide system. Rain forests are being cut down in order to make way for grazing land for cattle so that we may have beef for our fast-food chains. Canadians, as big beef eaters and big beef importers, are a part of this world-wide system that will mean the loss of rain forests.
Rain forests are crucial to the climate. Rain forests are crucial to the cycle that keeps moisture in the air. The destruction of the rain forests can mean a long-term change in weather patterns which again could mean that there will be even worse droughts than this immediate drought that is being faced now in western Canada.
We have to think about these things. They are not things that simply happen over which we have no control. We are a part of the world-wide community that is changing the surface of the earth and the surface of the earth reacts by setting up new processes. Some of the things we do have extremely negative long-term consequences. As responsible human beings, we must look at those consequences and consider what we can do to be productive and to use our resources in a fashion that will not deprive future generations of those resources and in a fashion that will keep those resources coming.
We need renewable resources. In agriculture, we are talking about productive soil. When agriculture began in Canada, the soil was very productive indeed. Productivity itself is declining through massive use of pesticides, chemical fertilizers, monoculture, not rotating crops and using crops that demand a great deal of the nutrients from the soil without replacing them or replacing them with more chemicals which are then taken out in the next crop year. We are beginning to get warnings about our agricultural practices through declining productivity and not very many of us are heeding those warnings.
There are some enterprising primary producers who are beginning to go into biological or organic farming, using methods that do not destroy the soil and view it very seriously as a renewable resource. I applaud those efforts. I am sorry to say that our own laws, tax provisions, subsidy systems, training programs and all of these things in which the federal Government participates by encouraging some practices and discouraging others at this time encourage the wrong kinds of farming practices.
Subsidies are still being provided for the kinds of agriculture that do not treat the soil as a renewable resource but as something from which one can get money right away by putting in certain ingredients, getting a crop out of it and then worrying next year about putting in more chemicals to make up for those that have been taken away in the past.
The decline of the family farm is a related concern. Family farmers, fewer in number in Canada, are very often in desperate situations. They are struggling to hang on. This drought will menace even more of them. Yet it is the family farm that is the best security for preserving the farming environment for the future.
Families do think of the future. Families are the means of reproducing for the future. Families see that young people grow up and inherit the farms. They have a very vital interest in seeing that the land that gets passed on to the next generation is productive and has the same possibilities for providing a livelihood as it did when the present generation inherited it. A family farm has no interest in simply killing off a resource, using it as a mine, taking out the nutrients and leaving nothing left for the future. We have a far better chance for developing a sustainable development approach to farming with the family farm.
If the family farm had adequate supports, it could do that. If the training centres and agricultural colleges and various kinds of assistance programs emphasized this, we would have an even better chance of seeing farm land used as a renewable resource, something very precious that should be kept productive, something that should be enhanced and not be allowed to be depleted.
I would like to make some remarks about the use of dams as a means for ensuring adequate water supplies for farming. Dams have historically been used to provide a water supply in a certain area for irrigation purposes. Certainly the immediate effects are favourable for a producing community. The effects may be unfavourable for those who are displaced, but clearly there is a positive impact on the people who are the beneficiaries of the new water sources in the new areas.
I think we must realize, however, that the long-term consequences of dams may not be as favourable as the shortterm consequences. There may indeed be very negative longterm consequences. If we are to use dams as a strategy for seeing that there is water, we must do this very carefully and after very thorough assessment.
Dams do interfere with natural processes. They see that water is kept in one place and does not move to another place. Dams see that certain lands get irrigated but the water has to come from somewhere else. We cannot simply assume that the beneficial consequences will flow to those producers without there being unfavourable consequences to other people because of the changes involved. We have not done nearly enough to assess those environmental consequences before those kinds of decisions are made.
May 9, 1988

We now have a water policy which provides that there should be no inter-basin diversions of water. I was pleased to hear the announcement of that, especially since we must be very worried about the trade deal giveaway of our natural resources. Perhaps water would be explicitly included as one of those things that could be given away. I would suggest, however, that some of us are not quite so happy that this water policy only remains a policy and it is not legislated. It is something that could be changed.
If water ever were treated as a commodity that could be simply sold south of the border, then, according to the trade deal, it could be treated as other resources and we would have an obligation to continue to treat water as a commodity. If any Government were so shortsighted as to do this, future Governments would not have the opportunity to redress that mistake. That, of course, is one of the real difficulties with this so-called trade deal, this giveaway, this loss of sovereignty.
Decisions can be made by one Government that will have an impact for the foreseeable future. The provisions that bind us, the provisions that mean that Canada cannot make decisions about markets, dispute-settlement processes or panels or commissions on which Canadians are only a minority will all bind future Governments as well as the Government of the day. That is why they are so very unfair. They do not allow for the political process.
A Government is elected and comes up with a policy which is not the right policy and it has to pay the penalty by being thrown out in the next election. However, with the trade deal, we may throw the Government out in the next election, but those decisions are entrenched in a treaty. It will be very hard to undo that. We cannot renegotiate it. We would have to get rid of the whole treaty, and the longer it would be in place, the more difficult that would be. The dislocations that would already be caused would be substantial, and we would risk even further dislocations if there were to be an abrogation of the treaty.
Water policy is one policy about which we must be concerned for the long term. I am not very confident about what the Government has done so far. It has certainly not managed to meet the concerns that I would want to see met.
Not only is there a question about quantity of water, we also have to be concerned about quality of water. The quality of water on our farm lands has been enormously affected by the use of pesticides and chemical fertilizers. This has an impact on drinking water. It has an impact on the water used for irrigation. What I do not think people have been adequately concerned about is the slow build-up of toxic substances in the soil and, through run-off, in the water system. Pesticides can get on the market because they do not have too toxic an effect on human or animal health when they are tested on lab animals at certain dosages. However, no one is looking at the long-term consequences of using those quantities of pesticides.
Supply
I asked a question about that in committee and I was quite disappointed to learn, although not entirely surprised, that the Department of Agriculture does not conduct any studies on the long-term consequences of using pesticides at present levels. I asked a question concerning running projections on the basis that the same quantities would be applied over 50 years or 100 years and what would the quality of the soil be. What would the implications be for the quality of water? No one has looked at that. The tests are only about the effect on a lab animal right now with these quantities. The chemicals used may only be a certain weight per hectare. It is not an enormous amount. The soil can absorb it. However, what if that same amount, even if it is only a teaspoonful per hectare, goes in year after year? These substances do not disappear. They are not broken down into helpful substances. Pesticides by definition are killers. Quantities can build up. Yet there has been very little attention paid to the long-term consequences.
What is our soil productivity going to be after 50 years of use of these chemicals? How safe is the water going to be in agricultural areas? Why are we continuing to approve these pesticides when we do not know how safe it will be after a number of years, even 10 years or 20 years, of use? Can we not have a Government that thinks a little bit about the future? I am sorry to say we do not. Fifty years or 100 years is just beyond its comprehension. It is thinking only about the next election and bribing the voters. It is not thinking about the long term.
That is just not good enough. If we are going to be concerned about sustainable development, if we are going to look at agriculture as a way for people to make their living and provide food to eat year after year after year, we have to take a longer term approach to the question. We cannot afford to simply say "no lab animals died this week from this pesticide." We have to look at them all together and think about the longterm consequences.
We have concerns about the quality of water and we must have concerns about the quantity. We have to look at the environmental decisions we make. We have to begin to think of the recommendations by the wonderful UN Brundtland Commission chaired by the Prime Minister of Norway. It brought together producing countries from all over the world, north, south, east and west, rich countries, poor countries, countries that use a great deal of pesticides and chemicals in their agriculture, and countries that do not. A rather amazing set of conclusions came from the deliberations of the commission. We all have to change our ways. The planet is at risk. We are threatened with being buried under the garbage created in our own communities. We risk leaving future generations with depleted soil, depleted fish stocks, undrinkable water, depleted but important non-renewable resources. Instead, we will be left with tailings and pollution in those communities.
It is a very sad fact that over roughly the last 100 years we have been using the earth in this extremely irresponsible way and getting rid of our resources and leaving pollution for future generations. The acceleration of the pace in the

May 9, 1988
Supply
Industrial Revolution, particularly after the last war, has been quite incredible. The result is that we are irresponsible citizens and the Brundtland Commission documented the abuses. Elowever, it also left us with some hope. The report says we can change. If we are going to survive on this planet we have to change. We have to change how we look at agriculture, fishing, forestry and all these other things. We have to look at agriculture as a renewable resource and we must integrate environmental questions with economic decision-making. When we look at the question of how we use pesticides, or whether we should be damming a river or not, whether we should be diverting water here or there, we have to look at the long term from the point of view of sustainable development.
I can see my time is up so I simply want to say that I have taken this opportunity to raise some of these long-term questions. I congratulate my colleagues who are raising the short-term questions and the tragic situation of the families involved in this drought. I certainly hope the Government will respond positively, listen to reason, and begin to devise some solutions to meet these immediate questions and at the same time begin to come to terms with the long-term need for sustainable development in agriculture.
