subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the resolution before us today concerns the emergency need for water supplies to deal with the drought problem in western Canada, and a long-term policy for water supplies for agriculture, clearly the Hon. Member who just spoke reminds us of the half-term report of the Science Council of Canada which indicates some of the dramatic and difficult problems facing our water supplies, even in Canada, for drinking purposes.
For example, the report, which came out last December, says things like: "The future is not bright". It refers to "a looming environmental crisis on a scale and depth of disaster far exceeding any met by earlier generations." This is in a country with some 10 per cent of all the fresh water resources in the world. It goes on to say that water shortages in southern parts of Ontario, Quebec and western Canada will grow, leading to more conflict among water users and demands for costly and environmentally damaging water diversions. It says that Canada will be caught up in a global water crisis by the year 2000. Half the world's population will lack adequate water supplies. It also mentions that Canada lacks a coherent science policy for water. Research is under-financed, students are not educated about water issues, and universities have failed to treat water as a serious field of study. It points out as well that the marine ecology laboratory and internationally famous research centre, the Bedford Institute for Oceanography in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, was just granted aid recently by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans.
I think the Hon. Member has raised some very important aspects of this whole topic. Although we are sort of looking at the need for water for crops, feeding cattle and emergency community water supplies in western Canada, it is not just a
regional problem for Alberta and Saskatchewan and parts of B.C. It is clearly a matter of national priority and national urgency.
I wanted to make these comments because I was reminded of them by the Hon. Member's speech in which she drew attention, not only to the volume and quantity of water, but to how important the quality of it is, not only for the growing of crops but for the feeding of livestock and the feeding of humans as well.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I welcome the comments of the Hon. Member. I share with him the concern that Canadians cannot be complacent. We indeed have abundant water resources, but we certainly do not have too much, certainly not with the use we are making of our fresh water resources right now. We do face the prospect of severe shortages in the near future because the water available cannot be used for drinking because it is polluted. Therefore, I welcome his putting on record the very particular concerns highlighted in this report. It is a long-term issue. Research must be done and we have to look for long-term uses.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my colleague who, like myself, spent some time this past summer in a part of the world where they have done miracles in terms of finding water and using it to grow things from almost nothing. The State of Israel has a computerized irrigation system for its orchards. It distributes small hoses to the base of each tree and, through the use of a computer, adds the exact amount of moisture needed in order that there is no wastage whatsoever.
Has the Hon. Member any examples from her research in environmental matters which indicate a methodology which we could use to more appropriately utilize what we normally think of as an over-abundance of resource but which is really finite on the planet earth? Has she any other suggestions from which we can learn on how to protect that resource?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the specific example given of computerized irrigation to ensure that this precious resource is used sparingly and in the best possible way. The very thrust of the recommendations of the Brundtland Commission report is that we have to get more out of less, that we have to stop wasting so much, that we must challenge our resources much more effectively. The report is very rich in practical examples of how we can get more out of less, how we can use fewer materials but better know-how in order to accomplish this.
As a general point, we must build into the decision-making on whether a particular project ought to be pursued the economic consequences through environmental risk. We must look not only at what will happen to one community, but at the community which will be deprived of that resource. We must not look only at what will happen in the here and now, but what will happen to the next generation. We must figure out
May 9, 1988

ways of costing this so that we will not continue to make mistakes. When we do something because it looks cheap right now, it means that someone else will have to pay the price in the future.
We need a different process. We must do our costing differently. We must build into the decision-making the costs to the environment and ensure that we do not continue to make the same kinds of mistakes as we have so far.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in pursuing the issue of getting more for less, would the Hon. Member care to make some comments about a number of different methods of damming water? One of the more popular systems which has developed in western Canada, and I guess other places in the world, is to go for the very large developments, to put in the very large dams. These are popular with politicians, I am sorry to say, and are not always as efficient as some of the alternatives.
There is a project in western Canada to which I will refer without giving its name. Local community farmers, ranchers, and environmentalists worked out a system of providing the same cubic acre feet of water through a series of 15 or 20 small dams across small creeks running into a river. They have saved the same amount of water for use by the rather scattered community. Wildlife has more access to the surface water under this system than would have been the case under the very large dam which was proposed, and there is much less likelihood of major damage to population centres if any one of them breaks. It is very unlikely that all 10 or 15 will break at one time, even if there is a flood situation.
As an additional extra, this seems to have provided a sponge effect over a relatively large area of the Prairies and has thereby maintained subsoil water supplies and the wells of some of the small towns and larger communities in the area seem to be benefiting as well.
Is this the type of interference by man which the Hon. Member has in mind when she speaks of getting more for less? Man seems to have drained most of the potholes in that part of the Prairies. Water used to go out very quickly down the rivers. It is now delayed and much is saved for use during the summer and future use.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again I welcome those comments and the very practical example of getting more out of less. We do have to learn the lesson that small is beautiful. Megaprojects are great for politicians; the bigger the dam, the bigger the bridge, the bigger the building to open, the bigger the ribbon to cut. All of this gives the taxpayer and the citizen the chance to see something big happening. Politicians fall for it all too often.
However, you can also get megaproblems from megaprojects and that is something which we want to avoid in the future. We should be paying far more attention to the careful use of this natural resource, respecting the diversity of uses, and respecting wildlife, something I did not go into. We must realize that agriculture has to coexist with environmental uses
Supply
of a different nature for the long-term preservation of both. If we really want to think to the future we must be looking at these varieties of uses.
The small projects, which can be extremely efficient and productive, are a far better way to go. Megaprojects have a dramatic impact but it is very hard to estimate their future consequences. One can find out too late that the project did not produce that which it was intended to produce, or that it has detrimental environmental consequences. One thinks of the Aswan Dam, a major project, the unfavourable results from which are just beginning to mount now. People are beginning to wonder seriously whether it was the right decision.
If we are humble enough and have enough respect for nature we will stick to smaller projects for using our resources very efficiently rather than bringing on the major problems which can be part of megaprojects.

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us today calls on the Government to provide both short-term and long-term solutions to a very serious problem. I do not have many farmers in my part of the world but the people who 1 represent are very close to nature and have suffered from time to time as a result of their livelihood being curtailed through the forces of nature. It seems to me that that is exactly what we are talking about today as far as the short term is concerned, possibly not as far as the long term is concerned, but certainly as far as the short term is concerned.
The evidence seems to be overwhelming that there is a serious problem with which we have to deal immediately. The precipitation in the Province of Saskatchewan has been declining over the past little while. It is quite obvious that it is a very serious situation, indeed. For example, the percentage of normal precipitation at the Saskatoon recording station is 83 per cent whereas from November 1987 to March 1988, it was under 70 per cent. That kind of ratio can be applied to other recording stations in the Province of Saskatchewan. The evidence is overwhelming that there is a serious and immediate problem as far as water is concerned.
I think there has to be an immediate solution found by the Government of Canada, but I do not think the solution should be a drain on other programs put in place for developmental purposes. I think there are adequate precedents and adequate funds within the Government to react to the situation. For example, there is an emergency response policy that was always there whereby there is a shared co-operation between the Government of Canada and the provincial Government. As I understand it, the province must put in the first advance of funds, something in the order of $.5 million or less. If that is done then the Government of Canada, if the situation is categorized as an emergency, can respond on a pro rata and shared-cost basis depending on the total nature of the bill. Those mechanisms are there now. They are available to the

May 9, 1988
Supply
Government. I think that is the approach which must be taken to solve the short-term problem rather than dipping into programs of a developmental nature which are designed, and should be used, for quite a different purpose.
I notice that the Government of Alberta, for example, has announced it will contribute. The Premier of Alberta has said he will provide help to rural municipalities and landowners suffering through this problem. There is money for building and rehabilitating dugouts and livestock water facilities, and so on. There is a certain movement on the part of at least some provincial Governments. The question now is if the federal Government will follow the lead of those provincial Governments which have made a contribution. Will it enter into a shared cost arrangement to solve in the short term this very serious problem?
In terms of the seriousness of the problem, we are told by the Alberta Agricultural Association that farmers want to seed by June 1. If they cannot do that, they might be able to plant barley, but they are sitting there waiting, debating whether to seed. A farmer, like a fisherman cannot go on with that amount of uncertainty. He has to be prepared for the season. If nature intervenes with an impediment, it has to be resolved.
These are questions we all face whether we live next to the sea or on the land. If we get our livelihood from nature, if we are primary producers, there will always be these accidents of nature which are going to have to be dealt with and which are no fault of the primary producers. That is what we elect governments for. We elect governments to deal with situations like that. It is easy to govern day by day when one can project what is going to happen three years down the road, but what is more difficult is to deal with emergency situations. But that is what governments are for. There is no way the individual farmer or fisherman can deal with a situation like this. It has to be dealt with by the Government. I believe that is what is needed here.
We are told, for example, that Ottawa may want to consider dipping into soil funds to ease the effects of drought in the West. As I said before, that is not the way things should be done. There is a need for the immediate resolution of the problem and there is a need for long-term development. I do not think we should take money from one to solve the other. There is a suggestion, for example, that the federal Government would consider taking money from the special $75 million soil and water conservation fund to help ease the effects of a drought in western Canada. I ask again, why do we have to dip into developmental funds? They are needed too. What is needed here is an immediate response from the Government. It has the funds and the mechanisms available to follow the lead of the provincial Governments and to respond in kind. That is for the immediate problem.
With respect to the long-term problem, I have to really support some of the things said by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald). Indeed, we do have a long-term water problem with which the Government has not
come to grips. There is the problem, for example, of acid rain. There has been a lot of talk about that but very little action. And there is the problem of soil erosion which is going on all over the world. I was able to travel to Ethiopia to see the kind of erosion going on there. That kind of soil erosion, to more or less of a degree, is happening everywhere. It is obviously not as serious in this country as in parts of Africa. It is a question of degree rather than kind. We must come to grips with that long-term problem.
There is another point to be made which I do not think is entirely irrelevant. That is the whole question of water supply. We are talking about a specific and immediate problem in western Canada, but there is also a water problem all across this country. I have villages in my riding in 1988 which do not have a supply of fresh water. In my opinion, there is nothing more important than that and there should be no higher priority. The Canadian Federation of Municipalities has asked the Government of Canada to join with it because there is now no federal program for participating in water problems anywhere in this country. There was such a program when the present Leader of the Liberal Party was the Minister of Finance and, hopefully, there will be again. We did have a program for contributing to water supplies but we do not have one now.
The Canadian Federation of Municipalities has asked the Government of Canada to participate with it because it cannot do it alone and some provincial Governments cannot do it alone, either, because in this country certain regions are richer than others. There are provincial Governments which would find it very difficult to get into the kind of expense that will be needed. Only the power of the purse of the Government of Canada can adequately respond to a situation like this. The Government of Canada has said to the Canadian Federation of Municipalities, no, that is your problem. Well, it is a problem. We have in western Canada an immediate problem and I think we have the ways and means to solve it.
I welcome this motion today. My Party has obviously staked out our position which was so well put by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), and I stand to give him some support from another part of the country, and to give support to those people who are so adversely affected in western Canada both in the short term and in the long term.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to discuss the water problem in western Canada. First, I should bring everyone up to date as to what my position is.
I have been a farmer since 1948.1 was born in the southwest corner of Saskatchewan and experienced what was really the drought of all droughts, the drought of the 1930s. My father was a blacksmith and the community ended up owing him something in the neighbourhood of $100,000. However, he could not keep his family any more so he decided to move up
May 9, 1988

to the northern part of the province to an area which is very similar to that which we see depicted in pictures in the Railway Committee Room. Most of the farms are covered in bush. The area was what one would call a homestead area. There were no roads. There was very little of anything. However, there was rain, growth and beauty. The move to that part of the province was well worth the time.
My father never did get paid his $100,000 or anything like it. However, he never wanted to go back to the part of the prairie where I was born. The memory I have of the prairie during the drought was of dust storms, grasshoppers and gophers-everything but green grass and growing crops. I was only too pleased to move to the area to which we did move. It has become a very productive farming area.
I must disagree that there is no long-term thinking in government. The Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) talked about pesticides, something which she hates. City people hate pesticides. However, they have come a long way, too, since the first ones were manufactured. The new ones leave less of a residue in the soil and are more efficient. They dissipate much more quickly than did the older ones. There has certainly been a big change in them. As time goes by I am sure that progress will be made in the use of various other types of pest control which may or may not be chemical. We are certainly going through a different type of control now that will be beneficial to the country in the long run. It has done very little harm to the soil.
As a matter of fact, in our particular area if we can get rain we can grow as good a crop now as we did when that soil was first broken. The control that we have over the weeds is of great help. Many people term pesticides chemical pesticides, something with which I do not agree. A great many of them do not hurt the soil but certainly help the farmers. Without them, all the government help in the world would not be able to keep the farmers in business.
Getting back to our long-term ideas with respect to what has happened over the years, I should speak a little about the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Administration, the PFRA. In the 1930s farmers were under siege. Early in the decade drought struck western Canada, turning the skies brown and the soil was blowing all over the place. I quite well remember that. The Great Depression plunged wheat prices from $1.25 per bushel in 1929 to 40 cents per bushel in 1932. That had nothing to do with the drought but with protectionism that was put in place by various countries. The opposite should have happened but because of protectionism that is the price to which grain fell.
In 1933 an infestation of grasshoppers destroyed crops. Again, I missed that one since I had moved to the north country where we do not have grasshoppers. They do not like a lot of moisture. We avoided that plague, and grasshoppers still do not like our country. In 1935 a rust blight struck the region, by which time the drought had spread to more than seven million hectares. We called them acres in our day. Between 1929 and 1937 some 14,000 farms in Manitoba, Saskatchewan
Supply
and Alberta were abandoned. If we keep these high interest rates up, we will have a lot more abandonments.
By 1937 the total value of grain produced in Saskatchewan was just 10 per cent of what it had been a decade earlier. That was partly due to protectionism. The federal Government responded with the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act in 1935. The purpose of the Act was to secure the rehabilitation of the drought and soil drifting areas in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and to develop and to promote within those areas systems of farm practice, tree culture and water supply that would afford greater economic security. Initial legislation allocated funding to PFRA for a five-year period. However, in 1939, the Act was amended to allow the agency to provide planning and assistance for soil conservation and water development over the long term. The PFRA became a permanent agency.
Now the PFRA has evolved to meet the needs of rural communities. On-farm soil and water conservation programs began in the 1930s. Large dam projects began in the 1950s, and municipal water systems began in the 1970s. The promotion of soil conservation began in the 1980s.
I return to what the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood said with respect to us not trying to improve our water supplies. The Government of Saskatchewan encourages dug-outs, small dams, and that so many acres are set aside for wildlife where there are beaver dams in order to create areas where the natural water level can be kept at the proper heights where conditions are available.
Today, as we grapple with the water shortage problem in western Canada the PFRA continues to play an important and relevant role. The PFRA now employs about 850 people. Its headquarters are located in Regina, with district offices in Winnipeg and Edmonton. It maintains a network of 21 field offices across the Prairies. Field staff provide how-to information to farmers seeking help with water supplies, soil problems, grazing space, water pumping and so on and so forth. I know that at the very moment it is very busy trying to fill dug-outs and municipal water supplies as well as water supplies to local villages and farmers.
One of the biggest projects that PFRA took up was the Community Pasture Program. Today that program has 87 community pastures in all three prairie provinces, mostly in Saskatchewan and Manitoba. They took over a lot of land that was badly eroded, that had suffered from wind and water erosion, and used the proper varieties of grass seed to fight the drought. They now have a good program going for areas that were once barren and caused a considerable amount of soil drifting and water erosion problems.
PFRA also took on a tree distribution program. Any Member who has been south of Saskatoon will see an example of many miles of trees that have been planted to keep the wind speed down. The trees have beautified the area, they keep the

May 9, 1988
Supply
snow in place, and also keep up the water level. This has helped a considerable amount with the shelter-belts. Last year
10.000	farmers received well over one million seedlings from Indian Head, and they continue to plant trees at a nominal cost, the cost of which is mostly the shipping involved.
PFRA has also entered into a soil conservation program. Over the long term it has made the land more resistant to precisely the type of wind erosion associated with the dry conditions now facing the Prairies. PFRA has revitalized its mandate for soil conservation by establishing a soil and water conservation service.
In 1984 soil conservation programs were launched under the five year economic regional development agreement with Saskatchewan and Manitoba. The federal share was around $8 million to the Saskatchewan agreement, and $4 million was contributed to the Manitoba agreement. Under these programs 45 soil conservation groups have been formed; approximately
2.000	producers have received almost $4 million in incentives for soil conservation activities. The PFRA soil conservation program in Alberta is jointly administered with the Alberta Government.
The PFRA is giving prairie farmers the hard facts about soil conservation. The present day farming techniques have been major contributors to salinity, erosion, and organic matter loss in the soil. The PFRA is working to create new attitudes about how prairie farm land can be best used. The PFRA is providing information about farming techniques such as continuous cropping and zero till. It conducts workshops, provides field tools and involves many other activities to spread the gospel of soil conservation.
We hope today's innovation will be a common practice tomorrow. The PFRA rural water development program is providing timely and substantial assistance on the Prairies to alleviate the current dry conditions. In particular, the well program is providing water supplies in many water-short areas. Rural water supply pipelines are carrying water to parched areas. Dams and dug-outs are widely used to trap water. In the Prairies, 75 per cent of the water supply typically comes from the winter run-off. This year the winter run-off was nothing. There was no snow in the southern part of the province. Therefore, that creates many problems because water has to be pumped sometimes as far as 10 or 15 miles.
Beginning in 1935 the PFRA had a program to encourage farmers to build dug-outs and stock watering dams. Since the initial year of this program the PFRA has spent well over $70 million on almost 200,000 on-farm water supply projects. Last year PFRA provided almost $5 million to help fund more than
5.000	individual projects. For some irrigation projects the PFRA will pay up to one-third of a farmer's cost. The PFRA also gets involved in group and community water projects. Hundreds of reservoirs constructed by the PFRA now dot the Prairies. Last year, it invested in more than 80 groups and community water projects. Under its current program the
PFRA will establish water supplies for groups of five or more farmers and towns with a population of up to 300. The costs are shared equally between the groups and the community and the PFRA.
While water is a natural resource, it is developed according to provincial strategies, the PFRA sometimes gets involved in large scale water related projects. It has contributed to building new water and sewage works in 49 towns in Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba.
The PFRA has played a key role in several major water projects. For example, the Bassano Dam rehabilitation project is assuring reservoir capacity meets the needs of area irrigation projects. Another example is the South Saskatchewan River project. Approximately 30,000 hectares is irrigated with water from Lake Diefenbaker. Irrigation has helped what was once primarily a wheat growing region to diversify. There are some problems with salinity because of irrigation. I know that PFRA is studying this problem and will be attempting to solve some of the problems created by the over-use of water in some areas.
The hydroelectric station at the dam site in Lake Diefenbaker is an important component of Saskatchewan water power. There is also a new dam that has been built very close to my farm which flooded a few acres approximately one mile from my farm. It will be beneficial to keep that area for the water that attracts the rain, and so on.
The sparse population of western Canada, its climate, and vast arable land has led to an economy based largely on natural resources, primarily agriculture. Soil and water are cornerstones of the western economy. They require careful conservation and development. Skilled management is essential. The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation program is certainly conducting some good studies and work in that particular area. That is a long-term program that has been very beneficial to the farmers in western Canada. It has done some exceptionally good work, and will continue to do so with the projects that it has and the projects that it is now starting out.
Drought is not the only problem in western Canada. It is my personal opinion that the biggest disaster to hit the farming community in western Canada was in 1982 when the Farm Credit Corporation was changed to become a bank. This was done by the previous Government with the help of the NDP. It allowed interest rates to follow the lending practices of the other banks. The Farm Credit Corporation is now the eighth or twelfth largest bank in Canada. This system of helping farmers has not been beneficial to the Farm Credit Corporation or the farming community in general. No industry can stand a 12 per cent or 15 per cent interest rate. At one stage of the game the interest rate was as high as 22 per cent. What we have today is worse than a drought. We have a situation where interest rates are the biggest bloodsucker to the economy in western Canada, and will continue to be so.
May 9, 1988

While Ontario is doing very well economically, that is not the case with the rest of the country. Western Canada is suffering as a result of high interest rates. In addition to impacting adversely upon the agricultural sector, high interest rates are having a negative impact in terms of business startups, thus affecting the broad economy.
We have to come to grips with the problem of high interest rates. More farmers will be chased off the land by high interest rates than by drought. If a farmer has to sell his crop for less than the cost of production, it is not possible for him to stay on the land. If we are to keep our young farmers on the land, we will have to bring about some changes. Under present conditions, it is not possible for the younger generation to carry on the family farm.
I met with one young man recently who is burdened by high interest rates. While he has been able to meet his payments to the Farm Credit Corporation thus far, he has had to do so through use of his operating loans, to the point where he is now faced with the situation where he can no longer make those payments. That young man now faces interest payments totalling some $32,000 in interest. There is simply no way that anyone can survive when faced with that kind of situation.
Mr. Speaker, I apologize for getting a little off the subject of the motion. However, the interest rate problem is one that is ever much as severe, in my mind, as the drought, and our planning has to address that question, as well as that of water conservation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the last three years I have been a Member of Parliament, I realized that Canadian agriculture was having serious problems, especially in Western Canada. As a member of the Standing Committee on Agriculture, I remember listening to representatives of farmers' groups, from the Prairies, who appeared before the Committee when we were looking at the possibility of drafting a report on farm input costs. At these hearings, the personal and very serious problems experienced by farmers and their families were also discussed, all the more poignant when we consider the pride of Canadian farmers who hate being dependent on government handouts.
Mr. Speaker, since the Hon. Member is very knowledgeable about his part of the country and is familiar with the wide open spaces of the Prairies we know that many farmers are at a considerable distance from urban centres, so when there are family problems, these are even more acute because there is no convenient access to services-I would like to know, since we in Quebec do not necessarily get the latest news every day, something about the human dimension of the present problems farmers are having because of the drought.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to answer the question.
Supply
It is difficult for one to describe the degree of social problem created by a drought, by a lack of water. For the most part, the agricultural sector is made up of family-operated farms, with the mother and the kids helping with the sowing and the harvesting, and it is a great disappointment for those families when they realize they are unable to meet the costs of the operation.
When confronted with a drought, the farming community suffers from an increase in divorces, in suicides, and in social problems in general, and high interest rates lead to the same situation.
We do have in place counselling centres for farming families, to assist in overcoming these problems. Certainly, this Government through its programs has shown that it is concerned about the problems which confront the farming community.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), on debate.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take part in this debate. It is not the first one I have been involved in since becoming a Member of this House in the fall of 1968. In that brief period, we have been through this type of debate on more than a couple of occasions. It is the same kind of debate that has prevailed since the West was first settled. There is nothing new about it. The Hon. Member for Mackenzie (Mr. Scowen), and the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), who is a south Saskatchewan boy, have both been there, and they know the score.
One has to ask when governments at the federal and provincial levels, regardless of their political stripe, are going to learn their lesson. When are we going to learn, from experience, that there will be cycles of drought; that there will be wet years and averages? That is the way Mother Nature operates. It has never been any different.
We continue to move from crisis to crisis. I can recall the spring of 1951 in Saskatchewan, when the southwest part of that province, along with southeastern Alberta, was covered with water. We thought we were into a flood comparable to that experienced in the days of Noah. In the main, southwestern Manitoba, all of the southern one-third of Saskatchewan, almost all of the southern one-third of Alberta, and the interior of British Columbia, chronically go through these cycles.
In the 1920s and 1930s there were many who asked that a long-term disaster fund be put in place. The view was that in years of good prices and good yields, the farming community would be willing to contribute to such a fund, with provincial and national governments also making annual contributions, thus enabling the fund to build to a point that it could be of assistance when disaster struck.
By way of example, the Western Grain Stabilization Fund went several years without having to be used. It built up, as I

May 9, 1988
Supply
recall, something near $3 billion but that has all gone now. In fact, it is in deficit. My friend says it has gone the other way. We had a billion or two dollars in it but now we are a billion or two short. But you must have something in place like that all the time, Mr. Speaker. When a disaster hits or when you have a period of drought for three or four years in a row, what do you do? You have what is called good, sensible, long-term planning, which you put in place and leave there. If you get lucky and go 15 or 20 years without a drought or without a flood, so much the better. We never seem to learn our lessons. I have watched successive governments in the provinces and in this House still refuse to do anything. They always do things at the last minute. It is the barn-door syndrome. As soon as the horses are gone, shut the barn door and see how we stop the horses from getting out again.
It is dry on the Prairies. One thinks of all the black humour. I am sure my friend from Victoria will know a lot of stories. There was one a few days ago. In several towns in Saskatchewan it rained briefly. Two and three year old children who were playing out in the yard ran into the house screaming in terror. They had never seen rain in their lives. It was so dry in one little town in southwest Saskatchewan, this farmer was getting a little elderly and he fainted in front of the post office. They brought him to by throwing a pail of dust on him. There is another story I have mentioned in the House. It was so dry that every time the wind blew the dust was so thick that the gophers were 10 feet in the air digging. In fact, the last time I told that one in the House was when our friend Mr. Whelan was Minister of Agriculture. We were in the middle of a drought and he said he was going to see how dry it was. I told him he did not have to go because I could tell him but he did not believe me. He went anyway but was still late helping the farmers.
How long are we going to take to learn our lesson? We do not learn from history. We keep on repeating it. We have weather records in detail back over 100 years in western Canada. The cycles are fairly consistent. It will have to cost, to begin with, the federal Treasury, a chunk of money. This will be in addition to moneys the Government has already put into the Western Grain Stabilization Program, in addition to moneys the Government will have to put in by way of a deficiency payment as long as that stupid price war goes on between the United States and the European Economic Community. So you are looking at $3, $4 or $5 billion a year in the coming years. That is the name of the game. It will not matter what political Party is in power sitting on the Treasury benches, it will have to be done. The question is not whether or not it will be done but when and how much. That is what the argument will be about.
We have been looking at figures for Saskatchewan and the efforts being made by the Saskatchewan Water Development Corporation. It is all great stuff, this farm dug-out pumping. Lay down a few hundred yards or a mile or two of pipe or hose and fill a dug-out out of the nearest river, creek or slough. Dug-outs have almost doubled, from 46 to 88. I do not know
but I think there are probably-I will get corrected by my colleagues if I am very far out-50,000 dug-outs in Saskatchewan alone. There are probably 100,000 dug-outs in the three Prairie provinces. It will be a little much to try to figure out how to try to pump water into them because mostly they are all dry.
Test drillings have done down. In 1987 we did 107. So far this year we have done only 93. What about deep wells? We had 26 last year and only 17 so far this year. As far as community wells are concerned, there were six last year and six this year. Then we have dug-outs and small reservoirs. We had 65 last year and we are up to 107 this year. Those efforts are all very worth-while.
Let me say to my hon. friend from MacKenzie who just spoke, if it does not snow in the winter-time and if it does not rain in the spring, those dug-outs, wells and reservoirs will be dry. It does not take a genius to know that. In fact, the water table has been lowered so much in the southern parts of the prairie provinces that drilling wells is tougher now than it used to be. You can drill all the wells you like, as worth-while an effort as that is, you have to try, but they will have to be deeper wells and a lot more expensive. Even if you were lucky and got an artesian flow, it might be enough for one farm, maybe two.
I suppose we could make the Prairies look like Swiss cheese and fill them full of holes. Surely it is not reasonable to expect that all levels of government and all the farmers could afford to drill enough wells to satisfy the water needs of every farm, every ranch in the southern parts of the three prairie provinces and the interior of B.C. Forget it, Mr. Speaker, you can't.
There will be years where there is no snowpack in the mountains. We had hardly any snow all year in Regina. The same situation applied to Moose Jaw, Swift Current and Medicine Hat. In fact, one day we got some snow in southern Saskatchewan and southern Alberta, about four or five inches, and a farmer thought just for the fun of it, as he still had a team of horses, that he would hook up the sleigh, go into town, get some mail and groceries and take the kids along. It was only four or five miles. Away they went into town, but the snow did not do any good. He was heading back home from town and one of those strong Chinook winds came up, blowing from the southwest, coming from the Crowsnest Pass and Lethbridge country. He had those horses going at full gallop. The Chinook was melting that snow so fast, the front runners were on snow and the back runners were on mud. That snow did not do very much good. It sank into the ground a little bit and a week later the dust was blowing again.
All the efforts we make with damns, reservoirs, dug-outs, well digging and everything else, you must have something else to protect farmers and ranchers from what is inevitably going to happen every few years in dry land areas. May I say that many farmers will have to smarten up about misusing their land. You will still find a farmer cutting down a bluff of poplar trees in the middle of a section of land where he should be
May 9, 1988

planting trees. Trees hold snow. They provide more moisture. They keep birds around, and birds eat grasshoppers. Farmers should not be cutting down trees. They should quit cultivating to the point where the top six inches of soil turns into the consistency of flour. A slight breeze comes and blows it into the ditches, filling them up. We should be into a major tree planting campaign, even greater than what we did during the Dirty Thirties and forties. I wish we could double or triple the tree nursery at Indian Head. It is not only the farmers but also the towns, villages, municipalities and Departments of Highways which need to pitch in in the name of soil and water conservation.
There is as well the matter of over-grazing. There is a guy in my province who has 96 or 100 sections. It's easier to keep track of them by townships than it is by sections. That land ain't fit for more than one head per quarter section, but it is over-grazed. In dry years, the deer might be able to survive because they eat the tops of the brushes, but no livestock can get enough feed to survive. Since it has been badly over-grazed in previous years, after the first one or two dry years, there is nothing left. The great sand hills begin to expand.
Efforts to combat those sorts of things have to be substantially enlarged by both the federal and the provincial Governments. We also have to begin to set up a real crop insurance scheme. Just because Mother Nature does things to us periodically does not make them disasters. If we have not learned our lesson from the way nature operates in Canada, we never will. It is not a disaster, it is the normal course of events. The climatic changes run in a pretty routine cycle of wet years, medium years and dry years, and it goes around and around, every 10 or 20 years. We need to have in place a crop, drought and flood insurance program with sufficient capital so that no matter what happens, even if there were a 10-year drought, we could cope with it.
We will be spending millions this year, unless we get some rain, moving hay out of Ontario and the Fraser Valley and the northern part of British Columbia down to the Prairies. We may even have to move hay from northern B.C. down to southern B.C. Farmers will be reducing their herds and that will cut the hog and cattle prices. Farmers will reduce their herds because they will not have enough feed, they will flood the market and down will go the price. They will be in the same rat race again.
This brings me to the whole issue of prices. I spoke to one farmer early in April. I said: "Well, what are you going to seed this year?"
He said: "I have concluded that I will save money if I don't put any crop in. I've got about 25,000 or 30,000 bushels in the granary, the wife's got a part-time job and I got a part-time job. I'll be money ahead to just fill my quota, make my payments to the Farm Credit Corporation and to the bank for the fertilizer and spray I bought last year, and just not seed a
Supply
bushel, not an acre. Let the damn weeds grow, and don't do anything with it this year".
I think that might not be a bad idea in some cases. Just do not bother putting in a crop. If there is some carry-over grain from last year and the year before, ride it out. Now, it is easy for me to talk. I am just relaying what one farmer said to me.
I know that there are other farmers who will need a lot more income than that just to keep their heads above water. Even if they do get a half-decent crop, unless there is a substantial improvement in the prices they receive for their product, they will continue to farm at less than the cost of production. I do not know of any other sector of the economy, except perhaps the fisheries sector, which experiences that. Only in agriculture and the fishery are we able to organize our economy such that they get less than it costs them to produce.
There is another old gag about the farmer who won $1 million in the lottery. They asked him what he was going to do with the money. He said: "I'll keep farming until it's all gone".
If you were to foist that principle onto the automobile industry, one can imagine what the big three automobile companies and the auto workers would do. If we were to tell them that they had to produce cars at less than the cost of production and the people who did the work had to get less money than it cost them to raise a family, we would have riots in the streets.
What would happen if we were to say to the financial institutions: "We are going to drive you money-changers out of the temple?" A fellow did that a couple thousand years ago, and they all snuck in the back door since. It needs to be done again.
When usurious interest rates are being slapped on to primary producers from coast to coast, it is no wonder that we have lost half a million farmers in the last 30 years. Where did they go? They went into the city. We didn't need any more in the city but we drove them out of a life they wanted to live. Our system drives people out of the kind of life they want to have. We stack the deck against them year after year. It is not a case of Conservative, Liberal or socialist Governments. Those are the kinds of things that any self-respecting national Government will damned well have to deal with. If there is to be an ideological war about it, the people of Canada and particularly the people of rural Canada will not pay any attention and will not vote for that kind of rhetoric. They want action and they want results.
Interest rates have to be reduced immediately. All the farm debts across Canada must be redone, and if that costs the banks a few million bucks each, tough cookie. They have ripped these people off enough for the last 20 years. They made profits in the billions of dollars and the big five did not pay a nickel's worth of income tax. Yet farmers write to me trying to get me to help them with an argument they are having with the income tax Department over a couple of hundred dollars.

May 9, 1988
Supply
The system has to be changed. It must have a fundamental change in its direction, its nature and its purpose. Without that, we will lose thousands more farmers. We will waste money trying to help them just barely make it. It will take them twice as long to go broke instead of half as long to get their heads above water and stay in business.
If this debate accomplishes nothing else, I hope that it has helped to concentrate the minds of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the President of the Treasury Board (Miss Carney) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). Nothing so concentrates the mind than knowing you are going to be hung in the morning. If they do not act, they are going to be hung one of these mornings.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to take part in the debate today, and I have listened very carefully to all Hon. Members who spoke to this Opposition motion. If we look at what is happening in developing countries, I am sure many people in this country would be astonished to hear we have a drought problem, a resource problem, a problem with soil erosion in a country as large and as productive as Canada. The problem is a very serious one. Emergency debates on the agriculture crisis have become more frequent, and today, throughout the world, negotiations are under way under the multilateral agreement referred to as GATT. I am sure that in the not too distant future, we will have to find the right answer to bringing Canadian agriculture back on its feet.
Today, Mr. Speaker, in connection with this debate, I would like to draw the attention of Hon. Members more particularly to the Canadian Crop Insurance Program. As you know, the Crop Insurance Act was passed in 1959 to enable the federal Government to help the provinces provide farmers with a form of protection, by minimizing the economic effects of crop losses caused by uncontrollable natural hazards, including drought.
The protection guaranteed under the Crop Insurance Program is available to all farmers who wish to take advantage of this offer, and applies to all Canadian provinces.
In recent years, this contributory program has played a vital role for insured producers. In fact, the federal Government's contribution totalled $181 million for 1987-88 alone. Today, crop insurance constitutes a safety net in case of disaster, offered by both levels of government to farmers. This shared-cost program is a vehicle of choice for the Government to provide producers with long- term protection, not just in emergencies.
This fact was also recognized when the Agriculture Ministers adopted the National Agriculture Strategy.
Crop loss assistance is generally a matter of provincial jurisdiction. However, the federal Government acknowledged
the need for helping the provinces through financial contributions to crop insurance programs, and in 1959, it passed the Crop Insurance Act, which was subsequently amended in 1964, 1966, 1970, 1971, 1973 and again quite recently, to improve assistance to farmers. The first province to acquire a crop insurance plan was Manitoba. By 1975, all ten provinces were equipped with a crop insurance program which is still in effect at this time.
A sucession of widespread drought-related crop losses struck Western Canada in 1983, 1984 and 1985. This led to a call, at the First Minister's Conference in November of 1985, for a concentrated effort by both levels of government to develop a national disaster-relief program. Following the conference, a federal-provincial working group was established to develop recommendations.
In January 1986, the working group presented its preliminary findings. It recommended, and the ministers of agriculture agreed, that crop insurance was intended to cover disastrous crop losses and that the program was doing a good job at a reasonable cost. However, the ministers agreed additional protection should be provided under the crop insurance program to meet widespread successive losses.
As an interim measure, the ministers recommended that the crop insurance program be enhanced in the western provinces for 1986, in areas most seriously affected by successive drought-related losses in 1984 and 1985.
The enhancement, called the "Multi-Year Disaster Benefit", took the form of additional coverage equal to 10 per cent of the average yield up to a maximum of 80 per cent.
In August of 1986, the working group presented its final report, which recommended that an enhanced crop insurance program be made available to producers in all provinces beginning with the 1987-88 crop year.
The recommendations were tabled at the Annual Conference of Ministers of Agriculture in August 1986.
The report became the basis for the section in the National Agriculture Strategy dealing with production risk protection and was signed by all Ministers of Agriculture and endorsed by the First Ministers in November 1986.
In response to recommendations, the Government made the following improvements in the Program: First, a large number of crops are now eligible for crop insurance. Second, programs for forage and feed grain have now been improved. Third, coverage has been added in the event of a natural disaster affecting farmers several years in succession. Fourth, the methodology has been enhanced for setting the premium rate and indemnity payments.
Mr. Speaker, the assistance provided by the federal Government and producer participation in the Crop Insurance Program make basic crop loss protection available to farmers
May 9, 1988

in the form of a production guarantee. Crop insurance is a form of long-term assistance offered by the federal Government. It plays a role similar to that of the fire brigade that rushes in when the neighbour's house or your own is on fire. The fire brigade is always on the alert and ready to help. Crop insurance is a little like fire insurance, and we are trying to encourage farmers to take advantage of this kind of long-term protection and assistance.
Deadlines for participating in the Crop Insurance Program are announced well in advance so that producers have plenty of time to buy the insurance. The guarantee applies to all farmers contributing to the Crop Insurance Plan, in all Canadian provinces.
The Program is very attractive to farmers. In fact, as I said before, federal contributions in 1987-88 totalled $181.5 million. During that year, 134,173 farmers insured 42,096, 702 acres of land. In Quebec, for instance, insured producers who were struck by a natural disaster received $21 million in payments, which included over $15 million from the federal Government. This protection is offered at a cost affordable to most farmers and taxpayers through government contributions. Producers pay only 50 per cent of the total cost of the program.
The guarantee provided is based on the principle of compensatory production for all fields of the same crop. Thus, when part of a farm incurs losses, it may be that with the aboveaverage yield of some fields, the total production of the farm exceeds the base production guaranteed.
Mr. Speaker, I know that my time is limited. In closing, I wish to say that we now have 230 crop insurance plans for some 87 kinds of crops in Canada.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the losses due to the water shortage that is now severe in the West are also covered by crop insurance and I am sure that with the sense of duty shown by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture when we intervened in March to solve temporarily, to be sure, the problem Western farmers were going through, with our Government's commitment, we will no doubt continue to play a leading role in Canadian agriculture.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 82-DROUGHT IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext: With the conclusion of this debate, the proceedings on the motion now before the House have expired pursuant to Standing Order 82(12).

A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 66 deemed to have been moved.
Adjournment Debate
TRADE-CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT COMPENSATE GRAPE GROWERS/REQUEST FOR GUARANTEED LINES OF CREDIT
["The motion to adjourn the House is now deemed to have been adopted. Accordingly, this House stands adjourned until tomorrow at two o'clock pursuant to the Order made Wednesday, May 4, 1988."]

Mr. Speaker, on April 25 I put a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) as to whether the Government of Canada would provide a line of credit for the grape growers who are being put out of business by the Government's free trade agreement.
This does not involve only growers in the British Columbian Okanagan Valley, but in the Niagara area as well. In fact, some 15 grape producers in Ontario have had to walk away from their farms because they could not get a line of credit. That information was revealed only on April 25.
A few days earlier a letter had been made public by Fred Somer who had been advised by the Kelowna and District Credit Union that they would no longer provide credit to him because, in their opinion, his financial resources in 1989, with the start of the free trade agreement with the United States, would in fact put him and the other grape growers in the Okanagan Valley out of business.
The letter from W. M. Redstone, the branch manager of the Kelowna and District Credit Union makes it very plain. It says: "Dear Mr. and Mrs. Somer: We refer to your letter of March 14, 1988, the communications we received from the federal and provincial Governments, and our subsequent conversations. Our concern is regarding 1989 and beyond. We feel reasonably assured that the 1988 crop will be purchased but income from that will only repay the operating loan, pay interest on the mortgage, and a small principal reduction. In 1989 you will have no income to service the mortgage interest and our security will be worth substantially less than the amount owing against it.
Unless you can provide one of the following which is to be acceptable to us, we regret we cannot make operating funds available to you in 1988 and we cannot pay any more cheques; additional security, compensation in the form of a lump sum reduction of the mortgage."
I spoke with Mr. Somer's son and he said that he had been on the farm for eight years and his father had been there for many years before that. Clearly it was the case that the Fred Somer family was the first victims of the free trade deal.
I asked the Minister whether, if the free trade deal is putting these people out of business, the Government would provide a line of credit. The Minister, of course, did not answer that. He usually does not respond directly to questions in the House. He talks about how great he is, how great the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is, or how many billions of dollars he has spent, but usually does not respond directly to any questions put to him in the House. In this case there was no change. He did not respond to whether the Government would provide a line of credit to the producers who are being put out of business and that is where the matter lay.

May 9, 1988
Adjournment Debate
It is interesting that the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) went to the Okanagan Valley a few days later. He showed a great deal of concern. The press report in the Toronto Star of April 26 indicated:
-Crosbie did say he would be "disappointed" if banks and credit unions
began refusing loans to grape growers for no reason other than fears over free
trade.
He was "disappointed". Mr. Somer and the other producers are not disappointed, they are devastated. They have hundreds of thousands of dollars invested in these vineyards and they are being put out of business. They cannot get a line of credit and therefore cannot look after their vineyards. There will be no crop and they will be destroyed by this action. All the Minister could do was mumble that he is studying the matter, negotiating with the provinces, and so on. However, as far as providing a direct line of credit to get them through this year until longer-term measures will be provided, there was nothing provided at all.
Although the Government has apparently made some representations to the Bankers' Association to support them, the Bankers' Association is saying "no dice" and essentially the Government is saying "no dice".
The Minister for International Trade talks in the newspaper article about visiting Kelowna. He said that in every arrangement there are going to be some winners and some losers. We have not learned of any winners. Certainly, the grape producers in Niagara and the Okanagan Valley are the losers. I think it is time the Government showed its goodwill to these producers who are being put out of business and provided them with an interim line of credit for the operation of their vineyards this year. If the Government is going to have a proper adjustment program, let it be put in place so that these grape producers know where they are going and know that the Government will stand behind its free trade deal.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by thanking the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) for his continuing interest in agriculture and particularly for raising the question of the position of the Canadian grape growers at this time. I certainly concur with the Hon. Member when he states that the Canadian grape growers and the industry they represent are experiencing difficulties. I do not, however, agree that the reason for those difficulties is solely as a result, or even primarily as a result of the free trade agreement.
As the Hon. Member knows, the grape growing industry in Canada has suffered for many years as a result of historical surplus production. Quite frankly, the federal Government has done its share throughout those years in purchasing that surplus production. In addition, of course, there have been some very real problems in the industry as a result of difficulties with GATT and a subsequent GATT ruling which, I am afraid, was anticipated by the Government and, I would suspect, by the industry as a whole.
During the course of the last eight years, the Government has been buying the surplus grape production even though it has recognized that that in itself is not necessarily a solution. Nevertheless, it was a type of assistance that the Government could provide. In fact, the Government spent some $ 13 million buying the surplus, and I am sure the Hon. Member applauds the Government's recent announcement that it will buy the surplus production in 1988, as it has done in previous years.
We believe that our efforts in buying the surplus production has given some degree of stability to the industry. Furthermore, we have on numerous occasions sat down with the industry and tried to address the problems that were anticipated with the GATT ruling. That is now with us and we are in the position, of course, of having to respond. The nature of that response will be very significant in terms of working out a long-term strategy.
With respect to the free trade agreement itself, I would suggest that the financial difficulties which exist in agriculture in general, and in the grape growing industry in particular, are not a result of a single year's events and not a result of a single development such as the free trade agreement. I think the difficulties which exist and which have been affecting those in the Kelowna area are the result of ongoing difficulties. Certainly the federal Government is committed to coming up with some sort of adjustment program. I too talked with producers in the area. I know how important it is that an announcement is made in the near future, and I anticipate that it will be.
FILM DISTRIBUTION INDUSTRY-EFFECT OF CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT/EFFECT OF AGREEMENT ON CULTURAL INDUSTRIES

Mr. Speaker, I am rising to continue with the question of culture on the bargaining table for the so-called free trade deal. It is not a free trade deal. It is not free trade because we do not have protection against the American countervail power. It is simply not free trade. It is much worse than that. It is a loss of political sovereignty. It is a loss of our power to make decisions and it is a loss of cultural sovereignty.
The film distribution scheme is perhaps the first casualty from the point of view of culture because of the shameful act of the federal Government in giving up on a promise it made to Canadian producers, directors and film people that there would be some improvement to allow for film distribution in Canada. It was not going to be Canadian ownership as recommended by a task force, but there would be a film distribution scheme. The Government abandoned that.
Last week the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) had the colossal gall to say that because of free trade not including culture this very minor measure could be proceeded with. The film distribution scheme recently proposed by the Government is a farce. It is a real capitulation
May 9, 1988

from the not staggeringly strong measure that it had proposed a year ago. It is still far from Canadian ownership.
The point is that culture was always on the table. It is not just film distribution. It is a whole lot of things. There would not be a section on culture if it had not been on the table at all.
Article 2004 is on intellectual property. Article 2005 is on cultural industries. Article 2006 is on retransmission rights. Obviously, the Americans did not have confidence that the Government would proceed with retransmission rights although it had already promised to do so.
Article 2007 is a print-in-Canada requirement. This is a sudden repealing of the sections in the Income Tax Act which define a Canadian issue of a newspaper or periodical for purposes of deduction of income tax expenses. In order to get this, as a result of this provision, the production has to be printed or typeset in Canada. There was a great row when this provision was brought in. The American Government protested it for a very long period of time. It was not clear that it would go through at all. Finally, it did go through. Here we have with a stroke of the pen a provision which has enormously stimulated the magazine industry in Canada and which is now going to be taken away.
Those are four very specific provisions. There are also a number of areas in which tariffs will be reduced on cultural goods.
Article 2012 deals with the definition of cultural industry. It says what cultural industries are. However, it is made very clear that printing is not a cultural industry. We could not have told Gutenburg otherwise, that printing was not a cultural industry. Thus the printing trade has been simply wiped off the cultural map in negotiations in which, clearly, culture was on the table. This is one of the items that got lost. It got traded away, although we have a printing industry in Canada and we want to keep it and stimulate it. This means that provisions that deal with school textbooks being printed in Canada in order to get on school lists will be against the free trade deal.
Articles 2010 and 2011 in this agreement are on monopolies. However, we do not call them monopolies. We do not call the CBC a monopoly. We call it a public broadcasting corporation. We do not call TVOntario or TV Quebec a monopoly. They are provincial networks for broadcasting. It seems to me that if the trade deal had been in operation back in the 1930s when the CBC was set up, it could not have been established. The same goes for TVOntario and TV Quebec.
The monopoly section of this deal says that whenever an American corporation can make money in the trade deal it has the right to do so. The Government may not set up a public service in that service area. Or, if it wants to set one up it has to go through a process, it has to notify the American Government that it wants to do so. It has to consult with the American Government, if the American Government asks it to do that. It may be taken to binding arbitration. If we agree to go
Adjournment Debate
to binding arbitration we would go there. If we do not agree we would be taken to dispute settlement. In the meantime there can be retaliation of so-called equivalent commercial effect, which means that Canadians would be set against Canadians. Extra tariffs could be placed on lumber, fish or some other product in order to punish us for taking an independent stance in the area of culture. Compensation could be ordered, and it could be ongoing compensation. This problem exists most importantly for our social programs. It could also occur for our cultural programs. There is no specific exemption.
When we look at the so-called exemption for culture, it is made very clear that it is only a partial exemption, that notwithstanding any other provision of this agreement, a party may take measures of commercial effect equivalent to those that in our case Canada took. In this way the United States could retaliate if we do something to protect our own culture.
This is an agreement that is the beginning of the end for our political sovereignty for Canada. It strikes right at the heart of our cultural identity. It is a shameful agreement. What is even more shameful is the fact that the Canadian Government will not square with Canadians about it. It will not even admit it is going on. It buries the most important provisions at the back of the agreement where it hopes that people will not see them. It does not even mention monopolies in the elements of the agreement. It sneaks these provisions in and hopes that Canadians will not notice.
I hope that Canadians will notice. I hope that Canadians will protest and fight for Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although I respect the right of the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) to interpret the free trade agreement as she sees fit, 1 simply cannot-and I say this at as a politician historian-concur with her assessment that the political sovereignty of Canada is in any way in jeopardy as a result of the agreement. However, the specific question before the House today relates to the cultural community and industry in general, and that is the point I would like to address.
We on the government side believe that our cultural industries are exempt from the free trade agreement, including Canada's publishing, film and video, music and sound recording, broadcasting and cable industries. The Government, as promised, has maintained all existing cultural support measures for cultural industries, as well as the ability to introduce new ones.
There are four specific undertakings in the free trade agreement touched upon by the Hon. Member. She identified them. We do not believe the ones identified by the Hon. Member have anything to do with the cultural role of these industries, and there are no other undertakings in the agreement which will apply to the cultural industries.

May 9, 1988
Adjournment Debate
The exemption for the cultural industries makes it clear that the free trade agreement will not in any way limit our flexibility to introduce special measures to assist these industries, as required now or in the future.
Last week the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) announced policies which were referred to by the Hon. Member in rather disparaging terms, with respect to new investment policies for the film industry and $200 million in new support programs to assist the production, promotion, and marketing of Canadian film and videos. The Minister also announced that she will shortly table legislation, as promised, to ensure that Canada operates a separate national distribution market. Through the additional funding and legislation to regulate the importation of films and videos, the Government has reaffirmed its commitment to the industry.
This policy was not negotiated as part of the free trade agreement. It is a Canadian solution to Canadian problems, developed in consultation with the film industry in Canada and around the world. Despite attempts by the Americans to raise the issue, Canada's cultural industries, including the film distribution issue, were kept off the bargaining table.
The free trade agreement will not in any way affect our ability to continue to develop cultural policies for Canada. In particular, the claim that the agreement will encourage U.S. retaliation against our future cultural policies is groundless. In fact, the opposite is true. At the moment the United States is free to take unilateral action against Canada in retaliation for what it considers to be unfair trade practices. The agreement will improve the situation, by placing some constraints on the ability of Congress to take action against any of our so-called cultural trade barriers. The United States will be required to demonstrate that a Canadian measure in fact contravenes the trade agreement. United States retaliation must be limited to a measure of equivalent commercial effect.
Furthermore, the U.S. will not be able to act unilaterally, as it can now. Advance notification and consultations with Canada would have to take place, in accordance with provisions in the agreement. The trade agreement is about trade, it is not about culture. It is a commercial arrangement that will put our economic relationship with the United States on a secure footing. Our culture can only gain from the stronger Canada that will result from this agreement.

ENERGY-LOW SULPHUR WESTERN COAL-PROPOSED USE BY ONTARIO HYDRO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that I do not have to remind you that yesterday was Mother's Day. I know that you are well aware of that, and I am sure you celebrated Mother's Day as people right across this country did. I am sure that all of us paused to reflect on that very special day and to think about that special relationship that you and I, Mr. Speaker, and all Canadians have or had with their mothers.
Unfortunately, my mother passed away about five years ago. Mother's Day always brings back those memories and those feelings of that special relationship. Many times I think of the qualities and the character that she tried to instil in me with her own way with those various lessons that she taught me. I think, as well, about those little things that make the mother-child relationship so special-and certainly occasions such as Mothers Day bring back one's childhood memories.
I often think of the nursery rhymes my mother used to repeat, and the one that comes to mind this evening is one she used to say when it was raining outside. Her purpose in saying it was probably to get me out of her hair. It went along the lines: "Rain, rain, go away, little Allen wants to play".
That is a rhyme that comes to mind every time it rains. I am one who does not like to stay inside when it rains. I much prefer to be outside enjoying the rain, whether it be a teeming rain, a thunder-storm, a steady all-day rain, or drizzle, or a mist. I am one who always enjoyed the rain. However, it is not something that I enjoy as much now, the reason being that when I am caught outdoors in the rain now, it not only takes the press out of my pants but causes severe health problems.
We are all aware of the devastation caused by acid rain in this country, and across the world. Our forests, our lakes and rivers are being severely affected, as are our buildings. As well, human health is severely impacted. We know that acid rain can lead to respiratory diseases and to certain cancers.
Acid rain is a tremendous problem for the world today, and it is one that all Canadians are well aware of. The only people in the world who do not seem to be well aware of the problem of acid rain are the Americans, who seem to think that acid rain is caused by bird droppings, or something of that sort. Some Americans do not seem to be able to come to grips with what this problem is all about.
Half of the acid rain that we experience emanates from U.S. sources, and our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has been doing his best, in the last few years, to try to deal with that. He has put acid rain at the top of the agenda with the Americans. He has talked to the President about it; he has talked to the U.S. Congress. He has done everything short of going to war with the Americans. As a sovereign nation, we know that we cannot force the Americans to reduce their acid rain emissions. Rather, we have to do so by encouragement, by negotiation.
The other half of the acid rain problem emanates from within Canada-and again this Government has made enormous strides in controlling acid rain emissions from within Canada. The federal Government has now entered into agreements with seven of the provinces to reduce acid rain emissions by 50 per cent of what they were in 1980, with the target date for that reduction being 1994. In addition, the federal Government has introduced strict lead emission controls for cars and trucks.
May 9, 1988

Perhaps the greatest source of acid rain emissions is Ontario Hydro, and that is the case because of the fact that Ontario Hydro uses high sulphur American coal to generate power, instead of the low sulphur Canadian coal that has been proposed as a substitute by our Government. It is because of the use of the high sulphur American coal that we have this enormous acid rain problem, and it is one that we cannot seem to solve.
A short time ago, you know, Mr. Speaker, and I know the Governments of the provinces and the federal Government set up an action committee to deal with this problem to try to find a way to bring low sulphur western Canadian coal to Ontario so that Ontario Hydro could make use of it, and reduce these horrible acid rain emissions very substantially. That action committee was made up of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), the Premier of Ontario, the Premier of Saskatchewan, the Premier of Alberta and the Premier of British Columbia.
I have not heard of very much action from this committee. We have heard all the excuses. We have heard that Ontario Hydro can get cheaper coal from the United States, so why shouldn't it buy cheaper? We have heard the excuse that all these long term contracts are in place with the Americans, so we have to keep buying this high sulphur coal from them, causing acid rain emissions in Canada. We have heard the excuse as well that transportation costs from western Canada to Ontario are so high that it does not make economic sense. We have heard all the excuses, but what we are looking for is action.
I would like to ask the Parliamentary Secretary when you and I, Mr. Speaker, and all Canadians can expect to get some action out of the action committee so that I can start enjoying those rain storms again the way I used to when I was a kid. How about it, Mr. Parliamentary Secretary? When are we going to get that action?

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for that non-editorial comment. "Jack Spratt could eat no fat, his wife could eat no lean, but together they licked the platter clean". I think that identifies the sense of co-operation which this Government has tried to bring to the country since 1984. It is because of that sense of co-operation in elements like the
Adjournment Debate
action committee that sometimes things are a little slower. It is easier in terms of speed to be a dictator, but it is not necessarily more secure in achieving what it is we would like to achieve.
It is particularly encouraging to stand in this Chamber today, and I speak as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, from Alberta, one of the places from where low sulphur coal might come and deal with a question by a Member from Toronto. The interests of the people of Toronto, the people of Ontario and central Canada do coincide with the producing provinces which have the low sulphur coal. British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, the Member mentioned, were involved in these discussions.
We are pleased in western Canada to hear that Ontario Hydro has made a commitment to reduce its emissions by 50 per cent over eight years, between 1986 to 1994 and that progress is already under way. In terms of action, 1 million tonnes of low sulphur western coal was bought by Ontario Hydro this year due to an unexpected demand. Original concerns about price are starting to diminish. The price of western coal and its deliverability-transportation is a big part of it-is starting to come down. One of the first initiatives our Government undertook was the deregulation of transportation, bringing in more competition. We are beginning to see this important commodity become more price competitive.
The Member asks specifically when we can expect action. I wish he would use the words "more action". There has been action. Meetings have been held. The Secretariat has produced a report on coal technologies which will now be the subject of a high level meeting of the action committee that I understand will be held in the very near future. We expect out of that to have some financial commitments to continue to work on those technologies which reduce price, help Ontario consumers, help the acid rain situation, and help create jobs in western Canada which will ripple back to eastern Canada with an increased capacity to purchase goods and services, equipment, supplies and materials. It is good economically. It is especially good for the environment and to be able to demonstrate in this country that by working together we can lick that platter clean and produce a better situation for all Canadians.
